My house has become a museum, everything inside a relic of my past, happy memories all turning to dust. The air-conditioning was switched off this morning so the house is stuffy. Jodie has been dead for three hours and I’m stepping into a different place, the ghost of the house that it was this morning. I wander through it, not really knowing what to do. Jodie’s stuff is everywhere and I can’t see myself ever packing any of it away. Her coffee cup is still on the bench, the bottom 10 percent still there, cold and manky. Toast crumbs form a trail across the kitchen floor. Makeup on the bathroom vanity, her towel, still damp, hanging on the rail. Jodie is missing and she’s here all at the same time, the house waiting for her to walk in, her husband waiting for the same thing. There’s an outfit lying on the bed; she must have been ready to wear one thing, then changed her mind. Jodie is always like that, she’s always one minute deciding to . . .
Was. It’s “was” now.
zh_text:
我家變成一座博物館，裡面裝滿我過去的遺物，快樂的回憶全部化爲塵土。冷氣今天早上就關掉了，所以屋裡很悶。茱蒂已經死了三個小時，我走進的這個地方不是家，而是早上那個家的鬼魂。我在屋子裡晃來晃去，不知道該做什麼。到處都是茱蒂的東西，我不覺得自己能把她的東西打包。她的咖啡杯還在長凳上，剩下百分之十沒喝完，又冷又髒。廚房地板上留下了細細一串吐司碎屑。化妆品在浴室的梳妝台上，吊桿上的毛巾還沒乾。茱蒂不見了，卻感覺還在，房子在等她走進來，她的丈夫也在等她走進來。床上有一套衣服，一定是她選好了衣服要穿，最後卻改變主意。茱蒂總是這樣，她總會突然改變心意……
以前是，「以前是這樣」。

en_text: “Jesus,” I whisper, and sit down on the edge of the bed. I pick up her top and hold it against my face and cry into it. What do I do with her clothes? Keep them? Give them away?
zh_text: 「天啊。」我低聲說，坐到床緣。我拿起她的上衣摀住臉，開始放聲大哭。她的衣服要怎麼辦？留下來？捐出去？

en_text: I don’t know when I’m supposed to think those kind of things, what kind of person it makes me for realizing it now. Do I do the washing and hang her clothes back up? Do I go to work next week? Do I leave Jodie’s clothes lying about the floor until after the funeral, then pack them up? My bosses at work don’t even know what’s happened. They know I went for lunch and haven’t come back.
zh_text: 我不知道什麼時候才該思考後續的安排，现在想這些事情，似乎不太恰當。我要把她的衣服拿去洗，然後掛回原處？下星期我要不要去上班？還是讓茱蒂的衣服躺在地上，等喪禮後再打包？公司裡的長官甚至不知道發生了什麼事。他們只知道我出外午餐，还沒回去。

en_text: I walk up and down the hallway—I just need somebody to tell me what to do.
zh_text: 我站起來，移到走廊的另一頭——我需要有人告訴我该怎麼辦。

en_text: I take off my clothes and lay them on the bed next to Jodie’s. A more creative man might study the bloodstains and find patterns in them, shapes of animals or boats, but all I see is my wife as she lay on the ground bleeding. They’re ruined. I roll them into a ball, then find myself coming to a complete standstill. I stare at them for a while. The cuffs are the bloodiest, then the arms, then the front. One of the buttons is missing. There isn’t any blood on the back at all. I straighten them out and hang them up.
zh_text: 我把衣服脫下，和茱蒂的衣服一起攤在床上。如果我更有創意，或許會細看血漬，找出有意義的圖案，比方說動物或船隻，但我只能看到我的妻子，躺在地上流血。這些衣服再也不能穿了，我把衣服揉成一團，發覺自己站著不動。我瞪著衣服看了一會兒。袖口上的血最多，然後是袖子，再來是前襟。釦子掉了一個。背後一絲血跡也沒有。我把衣服拉平，拿去掛起來。

en_text: I take a long shower, blood streaking off my skin, the penguin shower radio quiet as it watches me. I stare in the mirror at the large bruise on my face from the blow I took. The skin is slightly torn up, and one of my eyes doesn’t open fully—which I hadn’t even noticed until now. I don’t want to know this man anymore because this man got his wife killed. I picture it all happening over and over. I think about the bank teller, the way the shooter leveled his gun at her. Then I think about the 4 percent chance I came up with earlier when figuring the odds of Jodie being the volunteer, and realize it’s a false statistic since there wasn’t any probability involved. There would have been, if I hadn’t shouted out. If I’d kept quiet then Jodie would have had as much chance as anybody of living or dying—but I took that chance and turned it into a certainty. And why? Why the hell did I shout out? Schroder said it was to save somebody. Maybe that was it. Maybe I thought I could make a difference. Only thing I know is I was as surprised as everybody else—it didn’t sound like me and wasn’t the kind of thing I thought I’d ever do. Probably not the kind of thing anybody thought I’d ever do—the son of a serial killer trying to save a life. Well, Mission Accomplished. That woman is alive and Jodie is dead—I traded one life for another. This is what it’s like to play God, I suppose—but without the ability to do any good.
zh_text: 我在淋浴間裡待了很久，洗掉身上的血跡，企鵝收音機靜靜地看著我。我盯著鏡子裡的自己，被打的地方留下了一大塊瘀青。皮膚有點裂開，一隻眼睛沒辦法完全張開——我到現在才發現。這個男人害死了他的妻子，我想跟他斷絕關係。腦海裡不斷重播剛才的情節。我想到出納員，想到搶匪舉槍對著她的樣子。然後我想到那百分之四的機率，剛才我算出來茱蒂志願變成人質的機率只有百分之四，然後發覺我算錯了，因爲機率根本不存在。如果我沒有叫出聲來，何來百分之四。如果我閉緊嘴巴，茱蒂生存或死亡的機率就跟別人一樣——但我偏要冒險，讓惡果百分之百會出現。爲什麼？爲什麼我要對著搶匪大叫？施羅德說我救了一個人。或許吧。或許我以爲我能改變世界。但我只知道，我跟其他人一樣料想不到——我不是仗義執言的人，也沒想過自己會跳出來。或許別人也不認爲我懂得見義勇爲——連續殺人魔的兒子，想要從槍桿子下救人。好，任務達成。那女人活著，茱蒂死了——我拿一命換一命。我想，那就是所謂的扮演上帝——但我沒有能力行善。

en_text: When the phone rings it turns out to be a reporter. So does the second call. And the third. Before taking it off the hook I phone Nathaniel and Diana—Jodie’s parents. Nat answers and he’s already crying before I can say much.
zh_text: 電話響起，是記者打來。第二通還是記者。第三通也是記者。我決定先打電話給茱蒂的父母納森和黛安娜，然後再把電話拿起來。電話是納森接的，我還沒開口，他就開始哭泣。

en_text: “I don’t really know what to say, Eddie,” he says, his voice close to breaking. I’ve never heard him cry before. Nat, this solid, near-retirement-age man who could break a man in half, is weeping into the phone, he sounds like a child. “But we’ve been talking, and we think, we think that both you and Sam might, um, might be best staying with us tonight. Then she can stay with us tomorrow to give you a chance to . . . to get things organized.”
zh_text: 「艾迪，我眞不知道該說什麼。」他的聲音快啞了。我第一次聽到他哭。快要退休的納森體格結實，制伏一個人絕對沒有問題，卻像個孩子般對著電話哭泣。「不過我們談過了，我們想，我們想你跟小珊，嗯……今天晚上最好來我們家住。然後明天她留在我們家，你就有時間……出門辦事。」

en_text: “I don’t know. I think I need her here. All I know is that I have to hold her and tell her everything is going to be okay.” “It’s not going to be okay.”
zh_text: 「我不知道。我覺得我該帶她回來。我只知道我想要抱著她，告訴她會沒事的。」

en_text: “What the hell would you have me tell her?” I ask, the emotion on its way, pissed off at Nat now—but of course he doesn’t know what to say or do either, he’s just trying his best. “That our lives are going to fall apart?”
zh_text: 「那你要我跟她說什麼？」我問，對著納森發作我的怒氣——但是，他當然也不知道該怎麼辦，他只是想盡自己的力量。「難道要告诉她我們的生活一塌糊塗了？」

en_text: He doesn’t answer.
zh_text: 他沒答腔。

en_text: Five seconds go by. “Shit, I’m sorry, Nat,” I say, and I exhale loudly. “I didn’t mean . . . I . . . hell, I don’t know.”
zh_text: 五秒鐘過去了。「幹，對不起，納森，」我大聲吐了一口氣，「我並不想……我……操，我不知道。」

en_text: “None of us know.”
zh_text: 「没有人知道。」

en_text: “I’m going to come and get her.”
zh_text: 「我現在就去接她回來。」

en_text: “Are you in any state to look after her? Think about what’s best for her, Eddie. Come and stay with us tonight. It’s for the best. Then, then tomorrow you can . . . we can, together, we can . . .” He doesn’t finish.
zh_text: 「你現在能照顧她嗎？艾迪，想想看什慶對小珊最好。今天就來我們家住一晚。我覺得這樣最好。然後，明天你可以……我們可以，我們可以一起……」他說不下去了。

en_text: “She doesn’t know yet, does she,” I say, my heart sinking even more.
zh_text: 「她還不知道，對不？」我的心更往下沉。

en_text: “We wanted to tell her. And we were going to, but . . . I don’t know. It’s not that it was too hard, it’s . . . well, we thought you’d be the one who’d want to tell her. Diana and me, we thought it was best that way, if we were all together when we told her. For everybody.”
zh_text: 「我們本來想說，差點就開口了，但是……我不知道。不是不知道從何說起，而是……嗯，我們覺得你來告訴她比較好。我跟黛安娜都覺得最好我們三個人一起告訴她。這樣對大家來說都好。」

en_text: “You did the right thing,” I say, and I can hardly breathe now, it feels like a golf ball is lodged down my throat. “I’m on my way,” I say, and I hang up then take the phone off the hook.
zh_text: 「我同意。」我快喘不過氣來了，感覺喉嚨裡卡了一顆高爾夫球。「我馬上到。」掛上電話後，我把話筒拿起來，不讓別人打進來。

en_text: My car isn’t here. Jodie’s isn’t either. I phone a taxi company and a woman with no patience answers the phone and snaps at me, asking where I am and where I want to go.
zh_text: 我的車不在家。茱蒂的車也不在。我撥了電話叫計程車，接電話的女人一點耐心也沒有，厲聲問我要去哪裡。

en_text: I can’t seem to get any words out.
zh_text: 我一個字也吐不出來。

en_text: “Yes? Yes? You want to go somewhere, don’t you?” she says. “Or are you wasting my time?”
zh_text: 「喂？喂喂？你要叫車，不是嗎？」她說，「還是只想打來浪費我的時間？」「呃，我……我不知道。」我說。

en_text: “Umm, I, I . . . I don’t know,” I say. “Weirdo,” she says, then hangs up. I take a moment to gather my thoughts before calling another company, and this time I’m able to put sounds to the names of the places.
zh_text: 「變態。」她把電話掛了。過了一會兒我才能集中精神，打到另一家公司叫車，這次我就能把地址說清楚。

en_text: “Somebody will be there in ten minutes,” the woman says. “Have a nice day,” she adds, and I almost burst into tears.
zh_text: 「十分鐘後車子會到，」對方說，「祝你一切順利。」聽到她補了後面這句，我的眼淚差點奪眶而出。

en_text: The taxi takes me into the city. The traffic is heavy; people are all following each other too closely and trying to change lanes. The driver gives me a funny stare, and I know the one, it’s the one where he’s thinking, Is that the little boy, the one whose dad preyed on this city twenty and thirty and forty years earlier before and during and after he was born? Henry the homeless guy is still outside the parking building, a sandwich instead of a vodka bottle in his hand, the Bible still in the other hand.
zh_text: 我搭車到市中心。路上塞滿車子；一台車接著一台，還有很多人想切換車道。計程車司機瞪了我一眼，表情很奇怪，我看過那樣的表情，我知道他一定在想，這不就是那個小男孩？二十還是三十還是四十年前他還沒出生或正要出生或已經出生時，這男孩的爹曾危害過我們的城市？遊民亨利仍站在停車塔外，手裡的伏特加酒瓶不見了，换成三明治，另一隻手仍拿著聖經。

en_text: “Spare change?” he asks. He’s dressed in clothes made twenty years ago, with a baseball cap made from recycled cardboard, and there’s something about him that suddenly disgusts me even though he never has before. I have the urge to kick him. I look away and move quickly past before I can give in to the temptation. I run up the stairs all the way to where my car is.
zh_text: 「賞點零錢好嗎？」他問。他身上的衣服已經有二十年的歷史，頭上的棒球帽用回收的厚紙板做成，他身上有種東西突然讓我覺得很厭惡，以前從來沒有這種感覺。我有股衝動想踢他一腳。我轉過頭，很快走過去，免得我順從自己的欲望。我跑上樓梯，一口氣跑到早上停車的樓層。

en_text: I make my way out of the building, almost crippling a couple of other cars, almost clipping a couple of walls, driving perhaps too fast, perhaps even almost clipping a couple of people. I get onto the street and I’m two blocks away from the bank. I head in the opposite direction. Traffic is thick. I don’t see a single police car anywhere. I drive alongside the Avon where the grassy banks are heavy with food wrappers and empty drink cans, broken up by the occasional homeless person sniffing glue in the sun while working on his tan. The breeze is coming from that direction, picking up some cool air off the dark water. Traffic lights have broken down at a few of the bigger intersections, the orange lights flashing, drivers fending for themselves as they don’t know whether to give way or drive through.
zh_text: 把車子開出停車塔的時候，差點撞壞了另外幾台車，差點撞爛了幾面牆，速度可能太快了，也差點輾過幾個人。開到路上，離銀行只有兩個路口。我走向相反的方向。車子很多。路上都看不到警車。我沿著艾文河開，草綠色的河岸上丢滿了食物包裝袋和飲料空罐，偶有遊民在陽光下邊吸膠邊做日光浴。微風從河面吹過來，從深幽的水中帶來涼爽的氣息。幾個大路口的交通號誌壞了，黄燈不斷閃爍，駕駛人戰戰兢兢，不知該讓路還是該前進。

en_text: It takes me forty minutes to get to my in-laws. They look awful. They look like some creature came around and reached inside of them and ripped out every happy memory they’ve ever had. They give me tight hugs and tell me that we’ll all get through this. I hug them back and tell them nothing.
zh_text: 我花了四十分鐘才到岳父岳母家。他們表情慘澹。似乎有怪獸來過，把他們身體裡所有快樂的回憶都挖走了。兩人緊緊擁抱我，對我說我們能克服这一切。我也抱緊他們，但說不出話來。

en_text: Jodie’s parents have never approved of me. It’s not that I ever did anything wrong, or treated Jodie badly. It’s because of my father’s past. Her parents have always seen me as a loaded gun. They’ve always feared for their daughter. They tried to be pleasant, but they could never hide the fear that I’ve seen on other faces growing up—the one of suspicion. It’s been twenty years since my father was arrested for murder—that’s twenty years of having people around me always wondering, wondering, when’s Eddie going to become his father’s son? What is Eddie capable of? Jodie’s parents thought I was capable of slicing their daughter and granddaughter into a hundred pieces. Sum it all up, put a bottom line on it, and their fear their daughter would die at my hands came true.
zh_text: 茱蒂的父母一向不喜歡我。並不是我做了什麼壞事或虐待茱蒂，而是因爲我父親的歷史。他們老覺得我像已經上膛的槍，一直爲女兒提心吊膽。他們努力用笑臉迎接我，但總藏不住一股恐懼我從小到大就一直在別人臉上看到那種懷疑的神色。我父親因謀殺罪被逮捕已經是二十年前的事情這二十年來，周遭的人一直在思索，一直很納悶，什麼時候艾迪會變得跟他爸爸一樣？艾迪能幹什麼？茱蒂的父母覺得我能把他們的女兒跟外孫女切成上百塊。總而言之，到頭來，他們的恐懼實現了，他們的女兒死在我手裡。

en_text: Sam is asleep on the couch in the living room. I’ve seen plenty of photos of Jodie when she was a small girl, and right now Sam looks exactly the same. Her favorite teddy bear is clutched under her chin, her arm folded over it, holding it tight. I stand in the doorway and stare at her and my in-laws stand next to me and stare at her too. Nat has a key to my house—they must have swung by there first to pick up the teddy bear and probably some clothes. The plan all along had been for Sam to stay here anyway, so Jodie and I could go to my work Christmas party tonight.
zh_text: 小珊睡在客廳的沙發上。我看過好多張茱蒂小時候的照片，現在小珊長得就是那個樣子。她最愛的泰迪熊夾在下頷，手臂橫在上面緊緊抱住。我站在門口看著她，岳父母則站在我身旁，也盯著她看。納森有我家的鑰匙，他們一定先過去拿了泰迪熊，或許也拿了一些衣服。本來我們就計畫今晚要讓小珊留在這裡，我跟茱蒂才能去我們公司的聖誕派對。

en_text: “Let me make some dinner,” Diana says, and the words seem out of place and she knows it. I have no intention of eating. Probably none of us do. She has to do something, anything but stand still and let the terror get hold of her.
zh_text: 「我煮點東西給你們吃吧。」黛安娜的話似乎很不合時宜，她自己也知道。我一點胃口也沒有。或许沒有人想吃晚餐。她必須找點事情來做，不能光站在那裡等待恐懼入侵。

en_text: Sam wakes up. It’s slow at first, and then she sees me, and her face lights up. “Daddy!” she says, and she jumps up and has halved the distance between us. She’s six years old and that’s all she needs to be to immediately know something is horribly wrong. She can see it in our faces. “Where’s Mummy?” she asks, and her approach is cautious now.
zh_text: 小珊醒來了。一開始還迷迷糊糊，看到我的時候她滿臉放光。「爸爸！」她跳起身來，迅速拉近了我們之間的距離。她已經六歲了，已經能馬上發覺有些情況不對勁。看我們的臉色她就知道了。「媽媽呢？」她放慢了速度，姿態也變得小心。

en_text: I break down in tears and we do our best to explain.
zh_text: 我的眼淚奪眶而出，盡力向她解釋發生了什麼事。

en_text: The street has cleared somewhat, the onlookers having thinned out from lack of excitement. The media presence is still heavy, reporters desperate to catch more nuggets of gold with their cameras, probably the bodies being loaded onto stretchers. There is blood and glass and pieces of drywall and splinters scattered over the floor of the bank. Detective Schroder steps around them to the other side of the counter; Dean Wellington, the South Island manager for South Pacific Banks, follows him.
zh_text: 街道沒那麼擁擠了，旁觀的人群少了刺激也漸漸散去。留下的媒體依然很多，記者巴不得用攝影機撈到更多的金塊，最好是裝到擔架上的屍體。銀行的地板上有血跡有玻璃，還有灰泥和碎木屑。施羅德探長繞過地上的凌亂，到了櫃台的另一邊；南太平洋銀行南島分行的經理狄恩·威靈頓跟在後面。

en_text: “I still can’t believe this has happened,” Wellington says, his face flushed with the disbelief he’s feeling. “I mean, Jesus, what a mess. We’re talking about all that money, we’ve got damage to the building, we’ve got staff members ready to hand in their resignations, and this whole thing is a press nightmare. People aren’t going to want to walk through these doors for some time. James was a good manager, a good man, we won’t be able to replace him until after the holiday season. The timing of all this . . .”
zh_text: 「我還是不敢相信。」威靈頓說，他的表情恰如其分展現出他的不信。「我的意思是說，天啊，一團亂了。那些被搶走的錢，建築物受損，不少員工已經決定辭職，整件事上了新聞就是一場夢魘。短期內沒有人要走進這兩道門了。詹姆土的表現不錯，個性也好，但要等假期過去我們才能找到來頂替他的人。時機……時機就……」

en_text: “People died,” Schroder says.
zh_text: 「有人死了。」施羅德說。

en_text: Wellington adjusts his tie, pulling down on the knot and tightening it. “I know that, Jesus, don’t you think I know that? But this bank services thousands and thousands of people. We still have a responsibility to them, and you have a responsibility to find the men who did this. The bank wants its money back.”
zh_text: 威靈頓把頜帶結往下拉後收緊，調整了一下。「我知道，天啊，你以爲我不知道有人死了嗎？但銀行的客戶還有幾千幾萬個。我們對他們也有責任，你的責任就是把搶匪抓起來，把銀行的錢還回來。」

en_text: Schroder stares at him for a few seconds. “Just take me to the vault.”
zh_text: 施羅德瞪了他幾秒鐘。「帶我去金庫。」

en_text: The vault is near the back of the bank in a downstairs basement, two doors in between requiring swipe cards to enter. The metal door is about half a meter higher and half a meter wider than any normal door and made from solid steel. Inside, the vault is the size of a single bedroom. There are shelves stacked neatly with blocks of cash.
zh_text: 金庫在銀行後方的地下室，要用磁卡通過兩道門。金屬門比一般的門高半公尺，也厚半公尺，是紮實的鋼材。裡面的金庫大約是單人房的大小，一層層架子上整齊排著一疊疊鈔票。

en_text: “How much does this vault hold?”
zh_text: 「這金庫裡可以放多少錢？」

en_text: “Well, normally we’ll have a float of around a million dollars,” Wellington answers, “but this time of year, we stock up on more cash. We have to reload the ATM machine four to five times more often and people are always coming in for cash. Christmas is still a cash business,” he says. “Not everybody has a credit card.” “So how much?”
zh_text: 「嗯，通常流動的現金大概有一百萬左右，」威靈頓回答，「不過到了這個時節，我們會增加庫存的現金量。提款機補鈔的頻率是平常的四五倍，來提款的人也很多。耶誕節大家還是用現金的多，不是每個人都有信用卡。」「那大概多少錢？」

en_text: “About five million.”
zh_text: 「大約五百萬。」

en_text: “And how much was taken?”
zh_text: 「被搶了多少？」

en_text: “We still have to add up what’s here—but if you want a quick estimate, we think we’re talking somewhere around three million dollars.”
zh_text: 我們還得把剩下的錢加起來算算看不過粗估一下，我想大概三百萬吧。

en_text: “And the procedure in a bank robbery?”
zh_text: 「銀行碰到搶案的程序是什麼？」

en_text: “It’s simple. Do what the robbers tell you to do. Press the silent alarm, and if you have to come out to the vault, make sure you load in the dye packs.”
zh_text: 「很簡單。搶匪說什麼，你就照做。按下無聲警報，如果得進入金庫，一定要放自動爆破染色包。」

en_text: “And they loaded them?”
zh_text: 「他們放了染色包嗎？」

en_text: “Yes. They would have gone off by now.” “How do they work?”
zh_text: 「放了，现在也應該爆了。」

en_text: “They’re magnetic. We store them next to a magnetic plate that controls them. You take them away from that, and it activates a timer. They explode five minutes after they’ve been moved. It ruins all the money, covers it all in red ink. Covers the robbers in ink too.”
zh_text: 「原理是什麼？」「染色包有磁性，平常放在控制的磁性板旁邊。如果離開磁性板，就會啓動計時器。移動後五分鐘就會爆破，所有的鈔票就這麼毀了，沾滿紅墨水。搶匪也會沾滿墨水。」「要多久才能算出被搶的金額？」

en_text: “How long until you can get an amount?” “An hour. Two at the most.”
zh_text: 「一個小時，最多兩個小時。」

en_text: The blocks of remaining cash vary between orange, blue, green, and purple—fives, tens, twenties, and fifties. Schroder wonders exactly what three million in cash would look like physically. He wonders how heavy the bags would have been.
zh_text: 沒被搶走的現金有橘色、藍色、綠色和紫色，分別是五、十、二十和五十。施羅德心想，不知道三百萬的現金長什麼樣子。他納悶那些袋子有多重。

en_text: “So the tellers loaded the bags,” he says, thinking out loud.
zh_text: 「所以出納員負責裝錢。」他說出了心裡正在想的事。

en_text: “Yeah. Nobody else came back here.”
zh_text: 「對，没有其他人下來過。」

en_text: “The robbers never examined the bags, right? According to witnesses, and looking at the footage, they grabbed the bags and another victim and left.”
zh_text: 「搶匪沒檢查袋子，對不對？目擊者說，他們抓了袋子跟另一名受害者就走，符合監視錄影帶的内容。」

en_text: “So?”
zh_text: 「所以呢？」

en_text: “So why load the bags with hundreds?” “What?”
zh_text: 「所以，爲什麼要在袋子裡裝百元大鈔？」

en_text: “I don’t see any red blocks of cash—the hundreds. The bank tellers could have loaded the bags with any amount. The bags would have weighed the same. Why not load them up with five- or ten-dollar notes?”
zh_text: 「什麼？」「這邊都沒有紅色的鈔票，一百的。銀行出納員可以在袋子裡裝其他面額的鈔票，拿起來也一樣重。爲什麼不放五元或十元？」

en_text: “Maybe they thought the robbers would check.”
zh_text: 「或許他們以爲搶匪會檢查。」

en_text: The robbers would never have known unless they tipped it all out.” “Maybe they were scared and thought that was the way to go.” “Maybe,” Schroder says.
zh_text: 「或許他們怕死了，覺得該放大鈔才對。」「或许吧。」施羅德說。

en_text: “It’s a good point though,” Wellington says, “and something we might consider implementing in case, god forbid, this ever happens again.”
zh_text: 「不過這一點很重要，」威靈頓說，「或許我們該考慮加入相關措施，萬一，我說萬一再被搶的話。」

en_text: “You do that,” Schroder says. “And get me some amounts,” he says, and turns his back on the vault and heads upstairs.
zh_text: 「你看著辦吧。」施羅德說。「算出金額後告訴我。」說著便轉身離開金庫，走上樓梯

en_text: I was eight years old when I had the urge to kill my first animal. I was nine before I finally did it. It was about a month before my dad got taken away. I don’t know what created the urge. I think it’d been there all along, sleeping deep inside me, hidden—then one day woken. The police showed up at the house on a cold July day. The sun was out but had lost the battle to winter; the air was so icy cold, the mist that formed in front of your face when you exhaled could almost be snatched up and broken in two. It was the kind of day you didn’t want to get out of bed for. The trees were bare and the leaves had turned to slush on the ground, slush that would stick to your shoes, then get left behind on the carpet inside. It was a Wednesday morning. Usually the most exciting thing about Wednesdays was that they weren’t Mondays. Of course this Wednesday started out a whole lot different. It began with me standing at the window in my school uniform watching the police cars pull up, sure they were there for me, that somehow, in some way, somebody had found out it’d been me who’d killed the neighbor’s dog. I watched the cars come to a stop and men spill into the driveway, and I thought about running, just heading out the back door and jumping the fence, only I didn’t know where I’d go. No, rather than run, I would lie.
zh_text: 八歲的時候，我第一次感受到強烈的欲望，一定要殺死某隻動物。等我眞正下手時，已經九歲了。我不知道那股欲望從何而來，似乎一直存在我心裡，深深埋藏著，终有一天會爆發出來。在寒冷的七月，警察來了。雖然有陽光，卻抵不過寒冬，空氣冰冷，呼氣時臉前形成的白霧彷彿可以抓起來掰成兩塊。這種天氣誰都不想離開暖暖的被窩。樹上的葉子掉光了，地上的葉子爛成一團泥濘，黏在你的鞋子上，然後黏到室內的地毯上。那是星期三早上。通常星期三沒什麼可謗讚，只能說比星期一好一點。當然，這個特別的星期三一開始便與衆不同。一大早，我就穿著學校制服站在窗前，看著警車停在門口，確信他們爲我而來，不知怎地，不知道用什麼方法，有人發現鄰居的狗是我害死的。我看著車子停下來，數人走上我們的車道，腦海中出現逃跑的念頭，從後門衝出去，跳過圍籬，只是我不知道該往哪裡去。不，我不要跑，我可以說謊。

en_text: The police surrounded the house. They came up to the front door. I was crying when my mother answered it. I had moved into my bedroom and was standing behind the door, listening, shaking. The men came inside and spoke to my dad. I didn’t understand what was going on, why the police were coming to take my dad away for something I had done, and as hard as I tried to tell them the truth, I was too scared to say the words.
zh_text: 警察包圍了我們家，他們從前門進來。母親去開門的時候我哭了。我回到臥室裡，站在門後面傾聽，全身抖個不停。他們進來對我爹說了幾句話。我不知道發生了什麼事，不懂爲什麼警察要因爲我做錯事而把我爹帶走，我雖然鼓足了勇氣想說出事實，卻害怕到不敢開口。

en_text: I came out from the bedroom in time to see them put handcuffs on my dad. I cried harder. I wanted to confess but didn’t. I didn’t understand at the time, but the police had come for an entirely different reason—a reason that involved the niche my father had carved out for himself, one that included a list of prostitutes and a very specific hobby.
zh_text: 我走出臥房，正好看到他們爲爹上了手銬。我哭得更厲害了。我想認罪，可是開不了口。那時候我不明白，但是警察找上門的原因跟我想的完全不一樣因爲我爹爲他自己造了一座壁龕，建築在一長串妓女的名字和一個非常特殊的嗜好上。

en_text: I didn’t go to school that day. Instead my mum’s sister came to sit with me and Belinda while Mum went to the police station to learn what was going on. She was gone all day. A year later, after she was dead, her sister didn’t want anything to do with me or Belinda ever again.
zh_text: 那天我沒去上學。阿姨到我家來陪我跟貝琳達，媽媽去警局了解情況。她一去就去了一整天。過了一年，媽媽去世後，阿姨決定跟我和貝琳達斷絕關係。

en_text: I don’t know what kind of dog it was I killed in that month before Dad got taken away. It was certainly big enough, and dark enough, and most of the time angry enough. All it ever seemed to do was make noise. It’d howl at the moon and bark at the sun and growl at the breeze. The barks were high-pitched yaps that kept on coming, one after the other, scratching into my head like nails. The growls were low and threatening, scary, and the howls were long and painful. My neighbor never did anything to shut it up. Most times my neighbor wasn’t there. He’d leave this dog of his chained to a rusty old stake hammered deep into the backyard. If the dog was lucky he’d sometimes get food and if he was extra lucky then sometimes he’d get water for company. Neighbors would open windows and doors and yell at the dog to shut up, but the frequency dropped off over the years as they gave up. In the summer the yard was hard-baked dirt, cracked into jigsaw patterns, and in the winter it was dark with mud and cold with frost. The dog was too hot in the summer and too cold in the winter and one or the other during the months between. I didn’t know who to hate more, the dog or the owner, and in the end I hated them pretty much equally. The dog was hardwired to bark at things, and my neighbor was hardwired to treat the dog badly.
zh_text: 爹被逮捕的前一個月，我殺了那隻狗，我不知道是又大又黑，一天到晚怒氣沖沖。那隻狗似乎只會吵，對著月亮怒吼，對著太陽狂吠，對著輕風嚎叫。牠尖鋭的狂吠聲連續不斷，一波接著一波，就像釘子一樣刮進我的頭。嚎叫聲的音頻很低，散發出威脅，令人恐懼，悠長的怒吼聲則令人不快。養狗的鄰居從不想辦法讓牠閉嘴，反正他很少在家。他會把狗拴在後院裡深深敲入地下的生鏽鐵樁上。如果夠幸運，那隻狗有時候有東西吃，要是特別幸運，旁邊還會放一盆水。其他鄰居會打開窗門，對著狗大叫，要牠閉嘴，不過這些年大家都放棄了，愈來愈少人會開窗大叫。到了夏天，院子裡的土被囇得硬梆梆，裂開成拼圖的圖案，到了冬天則泥濘發黑，凍得冷冰冰。夏天對那隻狗來說太熱了，冬天又太冷，其他的日子不是太熱就是太冷。我不知道我比較討厭誰，那隻狗還是養狗的人，最後我恨人跟恨狗的程度應該差不多。那隻狗天生就愛叫，那鄰居天生就愛虐狗。

en_text: The urge grew slowly. I’d be at school staring at a math problem then suddenly I’d think about him, that dog, and I’d think about how great it would be if that dog could be divided into two. I’d get that thought a few times at school, and I’d get it plenty more times at home, and the thought never made me sick. At night I’d shake, my hands twitching as the dog barked, wondering why my dad didn’t go and do something. Of course I didn’t know it—but my dad couldn’t do anything about it. He couldn’t draw any attention to himself.
zh_text: 心中的欲望慢慢滋長。有時候，在學校裡盯著數學問題，我會突然想起那隻狗，然後我想，要能把牠剖成兩半，該有多好。這個念頭在學校裡出現了好幾次，在家裡出現的頻率更高，而且想到這件事時我一點也不覺得嗯心。到了晚上狗開始鬼叫，我會顫抖，雙手抽搐，不明白我爹爲什麼不想辦法處理這隻狗。當然我那時候還不知道，但我爹不可能去處理。他不能引起別人的注意。

en_text: The urge kept growing. It reached a point where it was never far from my thoughts. It affected my schoolwork. My marks were slipping, my homework was suffering—if things didn’t change I’d end up leaving school when I was fifteen and spend my life bouncing between being unemployed and unemployable. It seemed to me that the thing standing between me having the life I wanted and the life of cashing unemployment benefits was that dog. No matter what angle I attacked the problem from, I knew that as long as that dog barked I had no real future. I had to stop thinking about it. Day and night this desire to see the dog dead grew stronger inside of me, gestating, becoming a deep-seated need that was ruling my life.
zh_text: 欲望不斷膨脹，最後總縈繞在我的思緒中。學校課業也受到影響，我的成績退步了，我的功課愈來愈糟糕——要是情況不改變，我就會在十五歲的時候輟學，这一生不是找不到雇主，就是根本沒人要雇我。在兩種生活之間，唯一的障礙似乎就是那隻狗——第一種生活是我想要的，第二種則是我必須靠著兌現失業給付的支票過活。不論從哪個角度解決問題，我知道，只要那隻狗繼續叫，我就沒有真正的未來。再想下去，我就完蛋了。日日夜夜，心内想要狗死的欲望愈來愈強烈，不斷茁壯，變成一種根深蒂固的需要，主宰我的生活。

en_text: I told the urge I didn’t know how to kill a dog.
zh_text: 我告诉欲望，我不知道怎麼殺狗。

en_text: The urge, one night, found a voice and whispered back. It told me it was easy. It told me everything was going to be okay now. Then it told me how. My mother was the kind of woman who, when shopping for groceries, would stray from the list she had made and add what was on special, even if we already had plenty of the same thing at home. We’d have cupboards full of paper towels and flour and tins of food that wouldn’t fit in the pantry. Meat wasn’t excluded from this list—the freezer was always full, the exact quantity within its depths an unknown. I took a piece of meat from the freezer knowing it wouldn’t be missed. I hid it in the garage one morning before school, wrapped in an old rag and stuffed inside an empty paint container with a twisted lid. It thawed out while I studied at school and while the dog went about using up the rest of his barks. When I got home the steak was soft and felt fresh. My dad was at work, my mother was on the phone to her sister, and my own sister didn’t have any intention of shifting from in front of the TV. The dog was barking from two doors down. It was loud and consistent, but painful-sounding too, the barking of a dog who didn’t understand why it was suffering but didn’t know anything else.
zh_text: 一天晚上，欲望找到了聲音，低聲回答我。它說，很簡單。它說，一切都不會有問題。然後它告訴我該怎麼辦。我母親有個習慣，買東西的時候總忘了看自己的購物清單，看到特價就會亂買，就算家裡根本不缺那些特價的貨品。家裡的櫃子擺滿了紙巾，還有放不進食品儲藏室的麵粉和罐頭食物。肉也一樣——冷凍庫總裝得滿滿，裝了多少誰也不知道。我從冷凍庫拿了一塊肉，心想應該不會有人發現。有天早上上去上學前，我找了塊舊抹布把肉包住，塞在罐蓋已經變形的空油漆罐裡。上完課肉就解凍了，那隻狗也在那一天用完最後吠叫的機會。回到家的時候，牛排已經變軟，感覺很新鮮。爹去上班，媽媽在跟阿姨講電話，貝琳達黏在電視機前面。隔了兩棟房子，那隻狗還在吠個不停，很吵，人聽了也很痛苦，聽起來牠不懂爲什麼要受這種苦，但牠其實什麼也不懂。

en_text:
It took me only a few minutes to prepare the meat, another twenty seconds to walk to the neighbor’s house. I walked up the driveway and knocked on the door, the piece of steak wrapped in plastic and tucked into my schoolbag. I knew nobody was home, but I had a story planned in case somebody was, one of those “my ball went over your fence” kind of stories people hear every day in every neighborhood all over the world. Nobody answered. The dog was barking like crazy. I went around to the side gate and the dog lurched forward on his chain, lunging forward over and over, the chain snapping tight on his neck, strangling him as it pulled him back.
Sometimes it’d pull him off balance and he’d fall over, but he kept on getting up and charging forward again.
zh_text:
我只用了幾分鐘就準備好牛排，再花了一二十秒走到鄰居家。我走上車道，敲敲鄰居的門，包在塑膠袋裡的牛排已經塞到我的書包裡。我知道沒有人在家，但要是有人應門我也準備好了說法，比方說「我的球飛到你家的圍牆裡」這種全世界的人每天都會聽到的故事。沒有人來開門。
狗叫得快瘋了。我從側邊的門進去，被鐵鏈拴住的狗撲過來，牠撲了又撲，鐵鏈緊緊卡住牠的脖子，勒緊了把牠拉回去。有幾次鐵鏈讓牠失了平衡倒在地上，但牠一定會站起來，再度撲向我。

en_text: I took the steak out of the bag and threw it at the dog and he caught it in midair. He ripped into it immediately. He paused after a few seconds, took a step back, then sniffed at it, his suspicion of this last meal obvious in the way his jaw moved as if searching for what was wrong. It was the dog’s bad luck to be as hungry as he was, his bad luck to have an instinct tell him he needed to eat because he never knew when his next meal would come. He lunged back into the steak and, even as blood dotted the short fur on the side of his mouth, he kept chewing. The steak disappeared in only a few bites. Then the dog started running in circles. He carried on barking, but the barks weren’t as loud, and soon they turned into yelps. Still he kept running.
zh_text: 我從袋裡拿出牛排對著狗丢過去，在半空中就被牠接住。牠立刻大口咬下去。幾秒後牠停下來，往後退了一步，對著肉嗅了幾下，牠的下頜動來動去，顯然對牠的最後一餐有所懷疑，想找出問題在哪裡。可惜了，牠很餓，牠也很不幸，直覺要牠快吃，不然不知道什麼時候才能吃下一餐。牠再度對著牛排撲過去，即使嘴邊的短毛已經濺了幾滴鮮血，牠還是嚼個不停。咬了幾口後牛排就消失了。然後那隻狗開始繞圈跑。牠仍叫個不停，但是叫得沒那麼大聲，叫聲很快變成哀鳴。牠仍繞著圈子跑。

en_text: I ran too.
zh_text: 我也跑了。

en_text: The police were called the next day. The dog had died that night. Its owner had come home from a hard day of ignoring his dog only to find it lying in the backyard, quiet, its muzzle bloody—and in death the dog was shown a mercy it was never shown in life: it was taken to a vet. The vet took one look at the blood, opened the dog up, and went searching for answers and found plenty of them in the form of fishhooks and nails and thumbtacks that I’d squeezed deep into the steak. The police went up and down the street, knocking on doors, knowing somebody in our neighborhood had done it—hearing very quickly, I imagine, from the neighbors that everybody in the neighborhood had wanted to do it. It came down to who turned the fantasy into a reality. They came to our door and spoke to my parents, and I was scared then, but not as scared as I was when they came for my dad. They asked to speak to me and my sister, and I stood there with Belinda and told my parents and the police that I’d seen nothing, and the police thanked us all for our time and moved on to the next house.
zh_text: 第二天狗主人去報警。那天晚上狗就死了。主人一整天不理那條狗，回到家卻發現牠躺在後院，口鼻沾滿鮮血死了以後，牠享受到前所未有的慈悲：主人帶牠去獸醫那裡。獸醫看了看血跡，把狗屍切開尋找答案，發現答案就在我深深塞入牛排的許多釣鉤和釘子裡。警察在街上查訪，敲了大家的門，肯定兇手是附近的居民我猜，他們馬上就會聽說，附近每個人都想要那條狗死掉，問題在於是誰實現了這個幻想。他們也來過我家找我爸媽談話，我覺得很害怕，但後來我父親被逮捕時我覺得更怕。他們要求問我和貝琳達幾個問題，我們兩個站在一起，告訴爸媽和警察我什麼也沒看到，警察謝謝大家抽出時間來回答問題，然後就去下一家了。

en_text: Nobody ever questioned it. Not ever. Not even my mum. I was sure she’d notice the missing steak and figure it all out. I thought she’d call the police and they’d take me to a room somewhere and leave me alone until I pissed myself and cried and confessed. But she never did. Nobody ever did.
zh_text: 沒有人覺得疑惑，一直都沒有。連我媽都不懷疑。我本來以爲她會發現牛排少了，推論出我是兇手。我覺得她會報警，警察會把我帶到一個房間裡，把我留在那邊，直到我尿濕褲子，放聲大哭，承認我的罪行。但她沒發現，沒有人發覺。

en_text: Four weeks later my dad was arrested. A month after that my neighbor got another dog—he probably figured my dad had killed the last one so this one would be safe. And it would have been safe too if it hadn’t barked as much as the first one. He only had it a month before the same thing happened. The police came up and down the street and learned the same amount of nothing they’d learned the first time. My neighbor had had his fill of dead dogs by then and didn’t go about getting another.
zh_text: 四個星期後，我爹被逮捕了。一個月後鄰居又弄來一條狗一他可能以爲我爹殺了前面那隻狗，新來的狗應該會很安全。如果這條狗不像前面那條狗一樣叫個不停，應該安全無虞。新的這條狗只養了一個月，同樣的慘劇再度上演。警察在街上盤查，發現跟上次一樣一無所獲。鄰居受不了再死一條狗，從此放棄養狗了。

en_text: I have no idea why this story is in my mind as I drive home, or what it means. My psychiatrist way back then would have gone through entire prescription pads keeping me medicated if he knew. Seeing the way that dog died—that frightened me. I vowed that day as I ran home that I would never, ever do that kind of thing again. I made the same vow the second time too—and that time the promise stuck. I never told anybody about the urges. Certainly I never told my wife.
zh_text: 開車回家的時候，不知道爲什麼突然想起這件事，也不知道有什麼意義。很久以前的心理醫生要是聽到這件事，應該會找遍處方藥物，給我適當的治療。看到那條狗死掉的過程，我飽受驚嚇。跑回家的那天，我發誓我再也不會重複那麼可怕的行爲。第二次我又發了同樣的誓一從那之後我並未打破誓言。我從未把我的欲望告訴其他人。當然也從未告訴我妻子。

en_text: Sam is asleep in the passenger seat. The school holidays have begun and I don’t know whether it’ll be easier on her not going to school next week, or harder now that her mum is dead. I don’t know if the distraction of the classroom would have been a healthy thing or not. I don’t know how I can look after her during the weekend, during the holidays, during the next ten or more years until she moves out of home and begins her own life.
zh_text: 小珊在副駕駛座睡著了。假期已經開始，既然她母親去世了，我不知道不去上學是否能讓她更容易接受這件事，還是更難。我不知道用上學來轉移她的注意力恰不恰當。到了周末、寒暑假、接下來的十幾年内，到她搬出去開始自己的生活爲止，我不知道我能不能照顧她。

en_text: When I get home I’m hit with the expectation that something will be different. It’s as though all that happened today was a movie that’s rolled to the end, the gunmen only actors, the wounds on my wife manufactured with stage blood. If not that, then at least Jodie will be here somewhere, released from the hospital—on the way to the morgue somebody found her breathing and they saved her. I expect the police to be here, to tell me they’ve caught the men who did this. I expect life to have moved forward.
zh_text: 到家的時候，我突然心生期待，或許情況會不一樣。彷彿今天發生的事情只是播到結尾的電影，搶匪只是演員，妻子身上的傷口只是道具血。就算我猜錯了，起碼茱蒂在家裡的某個房間裡，已經出院了被送到太平間的路上，有人發現她還在呼吸，把她救活了。我期待警察在家等我，告訴我他們抓到了搶匪。我期待生活能繼續過下去。

en_text: What I get defies all my expectation—everything is exactly how I left it. Nobody has been; nobody is here, even the poltergeist who visits at night to mess things around hasn’t shown up. I step inside and between the time I left a few hours ago and now, nothing has altered other than the angle of the sun. It’s got lower in the sky, barely coming through the living room windows now, picking out dust floating in the air, and the temperature has cooled—but that’s about it. Mogo is somewhere else, outside somewhere, doing whatever it is that crazy cat does. Sometimes the voice from twenty years ago tells me there is a solution to getting rid of that cat. I wonder if Mogo senses that. I wonder, now that Jodie isn’t here, whether Mogo will ever come back.
zh_text: 打開家門，所有的期望都落空了——裡面的樣子跟早上出門的時候一樣。沒有人來過，沒有人在裡面，就連半夜來亂搞的搗蛋鬼都沒出現。走進前門，從幾小時前出門到現在，一切都沒變，除了太陽的角度不一樣了。空中的太陽下降了，陽光幾乎無法射進客廳的窗戶，空氣中的灰麈在光線中飛舞，氣溫也降低了就這樣，其他都沒變。魔菇在別的地方，應該出去了，不改他的瘋貓行爲。有時候，二十年前的那個聲音會告訴我，可以找方法擺脫那隻貓。我不知道魔菇有沒有感覺到。既然茱蒂不在了，我猜魔菇也不會回來了。

en_text: Sam wakes up when I carry her inside, but falls back asleep within about a minute. I get her tucked into bed and head out to the living room. I turn on the TV but the next news bulletin is still over an hour away. I tidy up the kitchen, putting the phone back on the hook, packing everything into the dishwasher, killing time, killing time—rinse a plate and—bang—another distraction but only for a split second before my world comes crashing back down. Doing the housework seems the wrong thing to be doing—but what is the right thing? It turns out the right thing is throwing a couple of dinner plates really hard into the wall. They both shatter. A small tooth-sized piece bites into the wall and stays there, the other shards raining down on the floor. I pick up a glass and it follows the same trajectory. Next thing I know half a dozen of them are down there, a cocktail of broken glass and ceramic shards, and I tip out the cutlery drawer and add to it before sitting down and leaning against the fridge.
zh_text: 我把小珊抱進屋裡時她醒了，不到一分鐘又沉沉睡去。我幫她蓋好被子，走回客廳。打開電視，但要等一小時才能看到下一節新聞。我清理廚房，把電話掛好，把要洗的東西都裝到洗碗機裡，消磐時間，消磬時間——洗盤子，然後——砰的一聲——我又開始胡思亂想，念頭一剎那就消失了，我又回到眞實世界裡。做家事似乎不對——那該做什麼才對？似乎我該對著牆壁用力摔盤子。兩個盤子應聲而裂。牆上嵌了一塊牙齒大的碎屑，其他的碎片如雨滴般落在地上。我拿起玻璃杯，循著同樣的軌道扔出去。不知不覺地，地上已經有六個杯子了，玻璃和瓷器的碎片混在一起，我拉開放餐具的抽屜，用力投擲刀叉，然後靠著冰箱坐在地上。

en_text: Sam is standing outside the kitchen. There are tears on her face and her teddy bear is tucked against her chest.
zh_text: 小珊出现在廚房外。滿臉淚痕，泰迪熊緊緊抱在胸口。

en_text: “Did you and mummy have a fight?” she asks, looking at all the broken dishes.
zh_text: 「你跟媽媽吵架了嗎？」她看著地上那一堆碎片。

en_text: “No, baby.”
zh_text: 「小寶貝，我們沒吵架。」

en_text: “Then why did she go?”
zh_text: 「那她爲什麼要走？」

en_text: I get to my feet and hug my daughter before taking her back to bed. I sit with her until she falls asleep, and I sit with her for a bit after too. I don’t know how to make it through the weekend. Don’t know how to plan the funeral. Don’t know how to plan my future with Sam. The truth is Sam’s the only reason right now I’m not picking up one of those shards off the kitchen floor and fishing for the veins in my forearm.
zh_text: 我站起身來，擁抱女兒，然後把她送回床上。我坐在床邊等到她睡著，然後我仍坐著。我不知道這個周末該怎麼過，不知道該怎麼規劃葬禮，不知道如何規劃我跟小珊的未來。事實上，如果没有小珊，我早就從厨房地板撿一塊碎片，尋找上臂可以割開的靜脈。

en_text: I clean the kitchen up, watching my wife reaching out over and over, the man behind her raising the gun, then I go back a few minutes earlier and watch us in the bank, I watch the men coming in behind her, different pairs going in different directions. I stand up and fight them, taking the guns off them, struggling with them, six gunshots and six gunmen all lying dead on the floor. People swarm around me and hug me, they recognize me, but the gene my dad gave me doesn’t scare them, in fact it excites them. The serial killer gene just saved all their lives.
zh_text: 我把廚房清理乾淨，腦海中不斷重現被持槍歹徒架著的妻子伸手求援的影像，然後我倒退了幾分鐘，看到我們坐在銀行裡，看到搶匪對著她背後走過來，成對朝著不同的方向前進。我站起來跟他們交手，搶走他們的槍，跟他們搏鬥，六聲槍響後，六個搶匪都躺在地上，死了。大家蜂擁而上，過來擁抱我，他們認出我了，但爹給我的基因並沒有把他們嚇跑，事實上他們興奮得不得了。連續殺人魔的基因剛救了所有人的性命。

en_text: Another time I grab Jodie and pull her back from the action, locking us into a nearby bathroom until they’ve gone. Then I watch as the men come in and the security guard takes action and he grabs the first guy, twists him toward the others, guns going off, the bad guys all shooting each other as smoke and blood fill the air. Then I picture us at lunch, laughing, planning, the time slipping away and suddenly we’ve missed our appointment at the bank, disappointed but alive.
zh_text: 或者，我抓住茱蒂，從現場逃走，躲在附近的廁所裡，等到搶匪走了才出來。然後我看著搶匪進來，警衛探取行動了，抓住第一個男人，把他一推，轉過去對著其他搶匪，槍掉了，壞人的子彈都打在自己人身上，空氣中滿是煙塵和血腥味。然後我看到我們一起吃午飯，笑語盈盈，計畫未來，時間悄悄溜走，突然之間便錯過了銀行的會面時間，我們很失望，但兩人都活著。

en_text: I picture getting a flat tire on the way to work this morning. I picture work piling up and me unable to get away. I picture a power cut, an earthquake, somebody choking on a piece of chicken at the restaurant, a car accident right outside work. I picture ringing Jodie and telling her I can’t make it, that it’ll have to be next week, and Jodie tells me what a pain in the ass I am and it’s obvious she’ll be pissed at me all weekend. I picture Jodie in the living room right now getting Sam ready for bed. The TV is on. Sam is asking for some cookies. Jodie is saying no, and Sam is getting upset. I picture reading Sam a bedtime story, something about elves and princesses, then Jodie and me sitting up watching TV, my arm around her, holding her, rubbing her shoulder and then she touches my thigh, I kiss her and then . . . she is gone. Dead. Her body bloody and empty lying on the road as the black van speeds away.
zh_text: 我想像，早上出門上班時爆胎了。我想像，工作多到做不完，我無法從辦公室腉身。我想像，停電了，地震了，餐廳裡有人吃了雞肉後噎到，走出辦公室時碰到車禍。我想像，我打電話給茱蒂，告訴她我到不了，要改期到下個禮拜，茱蒂罵我討厭鬼，看來一整個周末她都會生我的氣。我想像，茱蒂正在客廳裡，準備帶小珊上床睡覺。小珊想吃餅乾，茱蒂說不行，小珊就發脾氣了。我想像，我唸睡前故事給小珊聽，故事裡有精靈和公主，然後茱蒂跟我一起坐著看電視，我摟著她，她的手放在我腿上，我親了她一下，然後···她不見了。死了。她渾身是血，空空如也，躺在街頭，黑色貨車高速離去。

en_text: The phone rings. I stare at it but don’t want to talk to anybody. After eight rings the machine picks it up. Jodie recorded the outgoing message. Her voice in the silent house does two things simultaneously—it makes me think she’s still alive, and it makes me think her ghost is here. Two completely opposite things—and it does a third thing too—it makes me shiver.
zh_text: 電話響了。我瞪著話機，無心接起。響了八聲後轉到答錄機。留言是茱蒂錄的。在靜悄悄的房子裡，她的聲音讓我以爲她還活著，又讓我以爲她的鬼魂回來了。兩個彼此牴觸的想法而且她的聲音也讓我打起顫來。

en_text: “You’ve reached Eddie and Jodie and Sam, but we’re all out or pretending to be out, so please leave a message after the beep. ”
zh_text: 「您好，艾迪、茱蒂和小珊不在，也有可能我們只是假裝不在，请在嘽聲後留下您的訊息。」

en_text: The machine beeps. I’ll never change that outgoing message.
zh_text: 答錄機嗶了一聲。我這輩子都不會把這段留言洗掉。

en_text: “Ah, hi, Edward, it’s John Morgan here, umm . . . I’m calling because we heard about what happened, and, um . . . all of us here at the firm are feeling for you, we really are, and, and, ah, we wanted to cancel the Christmas party tonight out of respect—I mean, none of us want to celebrate anything at the moment now—but the place is already booked and paid for and most of us were already here when the news came in. Okay, I guess that’s it . . . well, there is one more thing, and I hate to ask, but this McClintoch file you’re working on, it really needs to be wrapped up before the break, you know what it’s like, and nobody else can really step in and take over because you’ve invested so much work in it, and we’d end up chasing our tails for the week, so, umm, what I’m saying is I need you to . . . no, wait, I mean I’m asking if you can make it in next week to get it completed? After the funeral, of course, I mean, there’s no way I’d expect you to come in before then—unless of course you really wanted to, say, if you needed work to distract you or something. Thanks, Edward. Well . . . ah, see you later. ”
zh_text: 「呃，嗨，艾德華，我是約翰·摩根，嗯……我打電話過來，因爲我們知道發生了什麼事，嗯……大家都很同情你，眞的，嗯，啊，爲了尊重你的感覺，我們決定取消今天晚上的耶誕派對——我的意思是，大家現在都沒有心情開派對——不過餐廳早就訂好了，也付了錢，聽到消息的時候，其實差不多全公司的人都在那裡。好，先這樣吧……對了，還有一件事，我很不想開口，但是麥克林多奇的檔案由你負責，一定得在放假前完成，你也知道，其他人都沒辦法接手，因爲你已經花了很多時間整理，要我們來做的話，一整個星期的時間也不夠，所以，嗯，我是說，我需要你……不對，我想問你能不能想辦法下個星期完成？當然要先舉行葬禮，我的意思是我不可能要求你在葬禮結束前就來上班——除非你眞的很想來辦公室，比方說用工作轉移注意力什麼的。謝謝了，艾德華。好吧……呃，再見。」

en_text: He hangs up and the line beeps a couple of times and I delete the message. I hate my job. Sometimes I can sense the people there wondering about me, trying to figure how many people I’ve killed, or how many I’ll one day kill, accountants inside all of them crunching the numbers. I slump in front of the TV. I have to wait until 10:30 for the news to come on. It opens with the bank robbery. The anchorwoman looks like she’s just come from modeling at a car show. She has only two expressions —the one she has for bad news, and the one for happy human interest stories. She composes herself with her bad-news face and recaps the highlight of the day, then says, “Some of these scenes may disturb.”
zh_text: 他掛了電話，答錄機嗶了兩聲，我把訊息刪掉。我討厭我的工作。有時候我會覺得同事偷打量我，想算出我殺了多少人，或者總有一天會殺多少人，他們心中的會計師細細咀嚼著數字。我癱在電視機前，必須等到十點半才會播放新聞。第一條報導就是銀行搶案。女主播看起來似乎剛從車展當完模特兒回來。她只有兩種表情——壞消息的表情，播報快樂人情味新聞的表情。她掛上壤消息的表情，重述今天最突出的故事，然後說：「有些畫面看了可能會讓人覺得不舒服。」

en_text: There are images from the security cameras. There is footage of the “after” by the camera crews that arrived. And there’s cell phone video footage from people too panicked to act but courageous enough to film what they could. The angle it’s shot from reminds me of the teenagers in the hoodies, and I’m pretty sure this is their footage, and I wonder how much they got paid for it, how excited they were about it all. It shows Jodie being dragged out of the bank, and even though I know what’s coming up, I still pray for it to go differently. Then it shows me coming out, chasing the men, five of them in the van, the sixth one with the gun, and late-night news being what it is these days where standards have relaxed enough where you can say “fuck” without being bleeped out; you can also see your wife getting shot too, because the footage doesn’t stop, it carries on as ratings are more important than and certainly more profitable than ethics, so the country gets to watch the blood spray from Jodie just as I got to watch it today, they get to see her knocked down, they get to put themselves in my shoes and see what I saw without feeling what I felt, and then they get to see it again in slow motion, the cell phone capturing everything in cell phone detail—not high quality, but high enough.
zh_text: 電視上播出了監控攝影機的畫面。有一段「事後」畫面是攝影記者到現場後拍的。還用手機拍的短片，那些人驚恐到不敢探取行動，卻有足夠的勇氣拿手機出來拍攝。鏡頭的角度讓我想起那些穿連帽外套的青少年，一定是他們拍的，不知道賣給電視台可以拿多少錢，他們一定興奮得要命。影片上的茱蒂被搶匪從銀行拖出來，雖然我知道接下來發生了什麼事，我仍祈禱會看到不同的結果。然後影片拍到我跑出來，追在搶匪後頭，五個人上了貨車，第六個人拿著槍，現在的深夜新聞反正沒有尺度問題，標準放鬆到髒話也不會被嗶嘽聲蓋過，意思就是，你也可以看到你的妻子被槍殺了，影片並未中斷，繼續播下去，因爲收視率重於一切，當然獲利也遠遠超過道德規矩，因此全國的人都可以看到血從茱蒂身上噴濺出來，就跟我今天目擊的一樣，觀衆看到她倒在地上，他們看到了我所見證的經過，但感受不到我的感覺，他們也能看慢動作重播，手機盡責拍下了一切細節——畫質雖然不高，但也夠了。

en_text: It goes back to the anchorwoman who, to her credit, appears momentarily uncomfortable by what the network aired. When she goes to speak she stutters over the first word. Thankfully for her career she recovers, and she’s able to offer up other details before segueing back to footage from the bank. There are sweeping shots of people in the street staring at the scene, shots of the police scouring the area, a nice, tight-cropped shot of me holding my wife, and no shots anywhere of the men who did this.
zh_text: 鏡頭回到女主播身上，她還算有良心，看了播出來的鏡頭後短暫顯現出不自在的表情。再度開口時，第一個字吃了螺絲。還好她立刻恢復正常，保住了事業，再繼續播放銀行的鏡頭時，也講述了更多細節。攝影機從四面八方拍攝街上瞪著銀行內搶案的民衆，拍到警察刷洗地上的血跡，近距離拍攝我把妻子抱在懷裡的樣子，卻沒有人拍到搶匪的模樣。

en_text: Then, when there is nothing left to show, it cuts to the people nearby when it happened—“we heard gunshots and ran,” “we didn’t know what to do,” “seemed unbelievable it was happening right here,” “we were almost killed.” Then come the interviews from people who were inside the bank. I recognize some of them. “They came out of nowhere,” “it was so scary,” “those poor people, my God, those poor people did nothing and got shot anyway.” A photo of a man comes up, he was the bank manager, he was fifty-six years old and had worked at that branch for nine years. It shows the bank teller whose life apparently I saved, her name is Marcy Croft and she’s twenty-four years old and has worked at the bank for nine weeks, and she’s shaking as the cameraman zooms in on her, and she says “He was going to kill me. I know that as sure as I know I’m never working here again. And that man, oh my God, that man distracted him and saved my life, and his wife, his wife . . . ,” she says, and she breaks down in tears and can’t finish but the camera doesn’t break away from her, it focuses on her pain and relief and the country watches her cry for another ten seconds before it goes back to the anchor.
zh_text: 然後，可以看的都看完了，鏡頭轉到旁觀民衆身上「我們聽到槍聲就跑了」、「不知道該怎麼辦」、「很難相信，居然親眼看到這種事情」、「差點就沒命了」。然後記者開始訪問銀行裡的人。有的面孔我看過。「他們突然就出現了」、「嚇死人了」、「他們好可憐，老天啊，他們什麼都沒做也被殺了」。電視上出現一個男人的照片，銀行的經理，他五十六歲，在這家分行九年了。然後出現那個說是被我救了一命的銀行出納員，她叫作瑪西·卡芙特，二十四歲，九個星期前來這家銀行上班，攝影機的鏡頭對著她拉近時，她全身顫抖，她說：「那人要殺我。我那時就下定決心我要辭職了。然後那個人，喔，天啊，那個人引開了他的注意力，救了我，可是他老婆，他老婆：」她放聲大哭，說不下去了，鏡頭卻仍對著她，她的痛楚和寬心，全被鏡頭然後女主播再度出現在螢幕上。

en_text: After the interviews a picture of my wife that I have no idea how they got—maybe from her work somewhere—comes up. Both victims have families, pain, and despair filling the spaces these people left. Then there’s me again, covered in blood, being led away from Jodie’s body. Edward Hunter, twenty-nine-year-old son of a serial killer. The anchorwoman mentions it.
zh_text: 訪問後，我妻子的照片出現在螢幕上，我不知道他們從哪裡拿到的可能是她同事提供的。兩名被害者都有家庭，他們留下的空洞被苦痛和絕望塡滿。然後我又出現了，滿身是血，被警察從茱蒂的遺體旁領開。艾德華·杭特，連續殺人魔二十九歲的兒子。女主播如是說。

en_text: The footage turns to a live feed from outside the bank. There’s still yellow crime-scene tape fluttering in the slight breeze. The spot where Jodie was killed has tape around it, and she’s been moved, and I have an image of her lying on a steel slab in a morgue, pale, grey, and blue and broken beyond repair, no longer covered by a sheet. The reporter has his sleeves rolled up, indicating he’s had a long day at work. He speaks for a bit, talking about me.
zh_text: 鏡頭轉成銀行外的現場實況。黃色的犯罪現場警戒線在微風中飄動。茱蒂被射殺的那個點旁邊也拉起了警戒線，警察把她搬走了，在我的想像中，她躺在太平間裡的鋼板上，膚色蒼白，灰藍藍，破損到無法修復，身上蓋的白布被移開了。記者挽起袖子，看似已經忙碌工作了一整天。他講了一段話，報導的對象是我。

en_text: “And Jack Hunter, of course, was arrested after murdering eleven prostitutes, isn’t that right, Dan?” the anchorwoman asks, the feed going back to her, her serious face on display.
zh_text: 「傑克·杭特，謀殺了十一名妓女後，當然遭到了逮捕，對吧？大丹？」女主播問，她又出現在螢幕上，神色嚴肅。

en_text: “Sure is, Kim. Of course that’s only eleven prostitutes that he admitted to.” “Has there been any speculation that Edward Hunter may have been involved?” Anchorwoman Kim says.
zh_text: 「對的，阿金妳說得沒錯，他認罪的只有那十一個妓女。」「是否有人推測艾德華·杭特也涉案呢？」女主播阿金問。

en_text: “At this stage the police aren’t commenting on that, however from what I’ve learned it does seem unlikely. I think for Edward and Jodie Hunter, and for the rest of these people, it was a case of wrong place at the wrong time. As soon as we know more down here in Christchurch, we’ll let you know.”
zh_text: 「目前警方不願意評論，不過，據我所知，似乎不可能。我很爲艾德華和茱蒂·杭特感到難過，其他人也是，他們不幸在不對的時間出現在不對的地方。如果基督城有進一步的消息，我們會立刻爲觀衆報導。」

en_text: Kim flashes her second expression at the screen, and then the image taken twenty years ago appears, of me in my school uniform by my father’s side. I almost throw the remote at the TV. The story gets to the climax—or, in this case, a punch line. The van was found. It had been stolen. No trace of the money. No trace of the people in it. The six men scattered into the city.
zh_text: 螢幕上的阿金瞬間閃過她的第二種表情，螢幕上出現二十年前的我，一身學生制服，站在我父親旁邊。我差點就把遙控器砸向電視機。報導到了高潮，或许該說是最關鍵的警告。貨車找到了，是贓車。錢不見了，人也不見了，六個男人分別躲到城裡不知何處。

en_text: I turn off the TV and sit in the darkness, wide awake, angry, hurting, and alone.
zh_text: 我關掉電視，坐在黑暗中，一點睡意也沒有，滿腔憤怒，飽受痛苦，孤單得不得了。

en_text: A man walking his dog called it in. He saw the smoke and called the fire department who rushed out before the blaze could spread out of control, latching onto trees and then maybe houses in the area, but not before the van could be destroyed. The twisted and charred skeleton is still smoldering, and Schroder knows any evidence inside is gone. There’s still forensic evidence, but that’ll take weeks—and even then it may lead to nothing.
zh_text: 報警的是個遛狗的男人。他看到煙霧，打電話給消防隊，在火勢蔓延到不可收拾或燒掉樹木或附近的房屋前，消防隊就趕到，把火滅了，但貨車已經全毀。燒得焦黑的扭曲車殘骸還有餘燄，施羅德知道車裡的證據都消失了。還是能找到法庭證據，可是要花好幾個星期，就算找到了也有可能於事無補。

en_text: The road is hard-packed dirt leading into a pine forest. The sides of the road are breaking up in areas from tree roots, patches of it blanketed in pine needles. About two kilometers from here in one direction people go mountain biking and jogging and horse riding, and two kilometers in another direction is the ocean, but right here the world is abandoned, and the men who came here knew that. The ground hasn’t given way to any impressions from feet, or from another vehicle. The man with the dog doesn’t remember seeing any other cars coming or leaving, and there isn’t anybody else to ask. He can smell oil and gas and the branches that have blistered in the heat. Halogen lights have been set up, pointing at the van, lighting up the nearby trees and creating hundreds of shadows among them. There is no breeze at all, and every thirty seconds or so he has to swat away an insect about half the size of a fly.
zh_text: 火災地點是條硬梆梆的土路，通往一片松林。路邊有些地方樹根頂出來了，路上有好幾塊地方蓋滿了松針。朝某個方向走兩公里後，是很多人騎登山車、慢跑和騎馬的地方，往另一方向走兩公里就能到海邊，但這裡則一片凄涼，把車開來的人也深知這一點。腳踩下去或把其他車子開過去，都不會留下痕跡。遛狗的人不記得到其他的車子開過來或開走，也沒有其他人可以問。他聞得到機油和汽油的味道，也聞得到在熱氣中燒到掉皮的樹枝。警方對著貨車架起了鹵素燈，照亮了附近的樹木，在樹木間創造出幾百個陰影。一點風也沒有，每隔三十秒他就得揮手趕走有蒼蠅一半大的昆蟲。

en_text: Schroder can’t stop thinking about Edward Hunter. He thinks about the dad, just your normal everyday average family man. All through the trial Jack Hunter with his smiles, his neat but cheap suits, never once appearing cocky or arrogant and certainly nothing like the insane person his lawyers wanted him to be. The defense told the jury that the dad heard voices, that he suffered from paranoid schizophrenia, that he could barely control what he was doing, let alone remember it. They said the voices took over, and when they did there was no Jack Hunter, but something else, something inside of him that was sick and twisted and had gone undiagnosed for years. The jury didn’t buy it. The jury liked the prosecution’s story better. That story went like this: Jack Hunter loved to kill prostitutes and he hated to be caught. Jack Hunter wasn’t insane, because he got away with it for too many years. An insane man with no control over his actions would have been caught sooner. An insane man could not have covered up the crimes the way he did and lived the way he lived. The jury bought that story and Jack Hunter got life in jail. End of story.
zh_text: 施羅德一直在想艾德華·杭特。他想起他的父親，一個稀鬆平常的居家男人。在審判過程中，傑克·杭特永遠面帶微笑，西裝雖然乾淨，卻很廉價，從不給人自大傲慢的感覺，他的律師要他表現瘋狂，他卻一點也不瘋。辯護律師告訴陪審團說他會聽到聲音，他有妄想型精神分裂症，控制不了自己的行爲，當然也不記得自己做了什麼。他們說他被聲音控制了，聲音變成主宰的時候，傑克·杭特就消失，但他體內的某樣東西會接手，很變態很扭曲，多年來沒有醫生診斷得出來。陪審團不信，他們比較喜歡控方律師的說法。控方的說法是：傑克·杭特喜歡害死妓女，他被捕以後非常不高興。傑克·杭特沒發瘋，因爲這嬮多年來他也沒被抓到。無法控制自身行爲的瘋子很快就會落案。瘋子不會像他這樣掩蓋罪行後還能照常生活。陪審團相信這個故事，傑克·杭特被判終身徒刑。故事就是這樣。

en_text: He can remember the image of Edward hugging his dad on the morning. Since reaching into the bathtub checking for Edward’s mother’s pulse a year later, he hasn’t really thought much about Edward. He remembered him again a few years later when he heard the sister had overdosed on heroin, but not since.
zh_text: 他還記得艾德華那天早上擁抱父親的情景。一年後，他走近浴缸，檢查他母親的脈搏，之後他其實很少想到艾德華。幾年後聽說他姊姊吸食海洛因過量而死亡，他又想起艾德華，接著就忘了他。

en_text: For the last few hours he’s been talking to witnesses and reviewing the security footage from the bank. The footage is video without audio, and it’s clear but not clear enough to zoom in on any of the bank robbers’ features. They can tell height and sometimes weight, but nothing more. However, not just anybody can successfully rob a bank, and certainly there must be some experience in the team that pulled this job off. At a minimum, half of them will have a criminal record for armed assault—and in all likelihood all of them will have a record for something.
zh_text: 他剛花了好幾個小時跟目擊者談話，反覆觀看銀行監控攝影機拍下來的畫面。監控錄影機錄不到聲音，影像雖然清楚，但要放大搶匪特徵時又不夠清楚。他們可以估算身高和某些人的體重，但僅此而已。然而，銀行不是你想搶就能搶的，這些人一定有些經驗，才能幹這檔子事。個搶匪裡面起碼有一半的人有刑事犯罪紀錄——很有可能六個人都有前科。

en_text: The next step is to talk to people in that world. Somebody somewhere has to know something—there’s no way these men won’t answer for what they did.
zh_text: 接下來要找那個世界裡的人聊一聊。總有人知道內情這些人不可能置身事外。

en_text: He watches the smoke spiral into the night for a while longer before getting into his car and driving back to the bank.
zh_text: 他看著煙霧盤旋上升，消失在夜色中，過了一會兒才開車回銀行去。

en_text: The funeral is on Monday. Jodie’s body was rushed through the backlog of bodies that were rolled in on Friday. They didn’t need to do much to her except take a hundred photos and go hunting around inside of her with a pair of tweezers searching for the shotgun pellets. Maybe they got it wrapped up since Christmas was coming. Maybe the funeral director freed up a spot so soon in his schedule because he’s heading to the Gold Coast for the holidays. Whatever the reason for the rush, I’m glad for it. The idea of Jodie lying in the ground isn’t what I’d call warming, but it’s certainly better than having her sliced up and exposed on a cold metal gurney in the bowels of the hospital morgue.
zh_text: 葬禮在星期一舉行。星期五有不少屍體被送入太平間，而茱蒂的遺體得到優先處理。警方不需要其他程序，只幫她拍了幾百張照片，再用鑷子從她體內挑出霰彈槍的子彈。或許聖誕節快到，他們也急著了結這件事。或許殯葬顧問空出了時間，因爲他準備去黃金海岸度假。不管別人在急什麼，我覺得急得好。想到要把茱蒂埋到地裡，沒什麼好高興的，但我更不想讓她躺在醫院太平間裡冷冰冰的金屬病床上等人宰割。

en_text: For everybody else, it’s a normal Monday. Others are off to work and the school holidays have kicked in, leaving thousands of unsupervised teenagers to drink beer and break into houses and steal big-screen TVs and game consoles. It’s summer and the world is moving on and Christmas shopping is in full swing with mall parking lots jammed full and parents fighting in line for the next best thing. It’s a stunning, bright sunny day, the kind of day I’m sure Jodie would have enjoyed, and if the choice was hers perhaps even the kind of day she’d like to be buried on. My bruises have faded. It’s been three days since the bank robbery, and all six men are still on the loose. The city is understaffed by police and overstaffed with criminals—the balance is out of whack and nobody seems able to correct it. Wednesday was to be my last day at work for two weeks, the same for Jodie. Instead she’s spending Christmas in a dirt plot and I’ll be spending it God knows where.
zh_text: 對別人來說，這個星期一跟平常一樣。其他人去上班了，學校開始放假，好幾千名無人看管的青少年趁機濫飲啤酒，闖空門偷竊大尺寸電視和電玩遊戲機。時值夏天，世界依然在轉，聖誕節的購物達到最高潮，購物中心的停車場一位難求，家長買不到最好的禮物，也要爭著買第二好的。陽光普照，令人眩惑，我想茱蒂一定很喜歡今天的天氣，如果她能選擇，或許她會選在晴天下葬。我的瘀傷退了。自從銀行搶案後，我的臉青了三天，六名搶匪依然在逃。這座城警力不足，罪犯太多——兩者比例嚴重失衡，似乎無人能夠解決問題。星期三本來是我最後一天上班，然後就要休假兩個星期，茱蒂也一樣。可是她卻要在土裡過聖誕節，我不知道我會去哪裡過。

en_text: I had to choose a dress for Jodie, and a coffin. Coffin shopping is something I never want to have to do again—different models have different specifications, the funeral director doing his best to guilt me into upgrading, as if a cheaper coffin would suggest to the world I hated my wife. Jodie’s parents took care of the flowers, the priest, the music, and the church, and everything else. There are probably a thousand things going on around me to make this happen and I wouldn’t know.
zh_text: 我得幫茱蒂選一件洋裝跟棺木。這輩子我再也不要買棺木了——不同的型號有不同的規格，殯葬顧問的話術巧妙，讓我充滿罪惡感，升級買更好的棺木，彷彿便宜一點的棺木會讓別人發覺我痛恨我的妻子。茱蒂的父母親負責鮮花、神父、音樂和教堂和所有一切。或许要做的事情有上千樣，才能完成葬禮，但我一無所知。

en_text: The cemetery is on the outskirts of town in a neighborhood where there are lots of trees and not so many houses and currently a large flock of seagulls circling above. There’s a church off to one side of the graveyard which has been abandoned since the priest was murdered there almost six months ago, but reopened in time for Christmas with the arrival of a new priest, Father Jacob. The church has one of those rare histories that few churches have, the history where nobody died in its construction. Love or hate religion, one thing is sure—it’s certainly leading the way in deaths. Religion takes more lives than cancer and coronaries and car crashes combined. A belt of trees form a barrier between the church and the closest of the graves; a couple of them have been cut down, fresh stumps surrounded by sawdust and bark jutting out of the ground, sun streaming between the gaps and hitting the stained-glass windows. A six-foot fence made up of iron bars with cobwebs and flaky paint stretches the distance between the cemetery and the road. Parked out front are a dozen media vans, nobody in them.
zh_text: 墓地在郊外，那區林木茂密，房屋不多，正有一大群海鷗在空中盤旋。一邊有棟原本已經廢的教堂，因爲主持的神父被謀殺快半年了，不過雅各神父及時到任，好讓教堂在耶誕節前重新開幕。這座教堂的歷史相當與衆不同，在建構期間居然沒有奪走一條人命。不論有信仰，還是沒信仰，只能確定一件事——碰到死亡時，只得跟隨宗教的引領。因宗教而死的人數遠超過癌症、心血管疾病和交通意外的總和。教堂和最近的墳墓之間有一列樹木構成屛障；兩棵樹被砍倒了，新鮮的殘幹旁都是木屑，地上橫七豎八有許多樹皮，陽光從隙縫中流出來，直射鑲了染色玻璃的窗戶。一百八十公分高的鐵棒圍籬上滿是蜘蛛網和剝落的油漆，從墓地延展到道路。前面停了十多台新聞探訪車，車裡沒有人。

en_text: Father Jacob has a deep voice that sounds somber, the acoustics of the church helping him convey the depths of his words—which to me all sound hollow. He stands up at a podium a few meters from my wife, looking more like a wizard than a priest, his white hair in need of a trim, an outfit one might wear to a fancy dress party. He tells us about God, and Heaven, and I’m not real sure where I stand on those concepts right now. My grandparents raised me to believe in God, but these were the same people who raised my dad, and look how he turned out. I want to believe in something; it would mean Jodie is somewhere better than this world—and she is certainly somewhere better than Christchurch. And I want to believe in something to make it easier on Sam. I’ve thought about it a lot over the last few days, and I think it comes down to this—I want to believe in God, but right now I’m too damn angry with Him to do so.
zh_text: 雅各神父的聲音低沉，聽起來很抑鬱，教堂的音響效果幫他傳達言語中的深意——但我聽了卻覺得空洞。他站在離我妻子幾公尺遠的講台上，外表比較像巫師，不像神父，白髮需要修剪，衣著很適合穿去化裝舞會。他提到上帝，提到天堂，我不太確定我現在對上帝和天堂有什麼想法。祖父母把我養大，要我相信上帝，但他們也負責養育我爹，看看他現在變成什麼樣！我想要信仰；我才能相信茱蒂去了一個更好的地方——絕對比基督城更好。我要有信仰，才能慢慢讓小珊接受現實。過去幾年我想了又想，我想到的答案就是我要相信上帝，不過現在我氣到不想理衪了。

en_text: It’s almost thirty-five degrees outside, but it’s cool in the church, and it’s obvious I’m not the only one who feels it. There is something bad inside this place, maybe the same bad thing that got the previous priest murdered, or perhaps it’s the ghost of that priest himself, still here, watching over us. I wonder if Father Jacob senses it, whether he wonders if he’ll be the next priest to come to a dark end.
zh_text: 外面幾乎有三十五度，但教堂內很涼爽，顯然大家都有一樣的感受。這地方有股邪氣，或許就是這股邪氣害前任神父被殺，或許邪氣就是那被殺神父的鬼魂，仍在這裡看著我們。不知道雅各神父感覺到了沒，不知道他是否納悶自己會是下一個不得好死的神父。

en_text: A lot of people show up—I never knew that I knew that many people. They show up from the firm I work at. There are plenty from Jodie’s firm too, and of course it’s not like we were social lepers, which means all our friends and family are here too. There are people I don’t recognize, others I haven’t seen in a long, long time. No one really knows what to say—except for John Morgan, who shakes my hand and reminds me, when I get the chance, to head in tomorrow and Wednesday to finish off the McClintoch file. I smile at him and think about putting him in a coffin of his own.
zh_text: 來了好多人——我從不知道我認識這麼多人。有些是我的同事，有些是茱蒂的同事，當然我們沒有什麼社交問題，所以親朋好友都來了。有些人我不認識，有些人好久好久沒看到了。沒有人確切知道該說什麼，除了約翰·摩根以外，他握了我的手，提醒我有空的話明後天就進辦公室做完麥克林多奇的案子。我對他微微一笑，想找具棺木把他塞進去。

en_text: I don’t have any family—my grandparents, who raised me and Belinda after Mum died, are both dead: a heart attack got my granddad; pneumonia and complications but mostly loneliness got my grandmother not long after. More than anybody, I wish Belinda was here. When we were young, before Dad got taken away, Belinda did her best to pretend I didn’t exist, and when she couldn’t pretend hard enough to make me disappear, she’d begrudgingly throw the occasional sentence my way. When we found out what Dad had done, she spoke to me more but her words were harsher. Then when we found Mum dead in the bathtub, she held my hand and stroked my hair while we waited for the police to arrive. She told me that day that she loved me, and that she would take care of me. Of course our grandparents ended up taking care of both of us, but it was a struggle for them. They were old and didn’t really have the means to support us that well, but they did what they could to keep us from being put into foster care. Belinda always saw me as her responsibility. She was four years older than me, a big sister and mum all wrapped into one person, but at night she was neither of those—at night she used to sneak out of home and work the streets for money, and she’d come back crying with her pockets full of dirty banknotes and she’d hug me and tell me everything was going to be okay. Eventually it wasn’t okay for her—she hated what she was doing, and the only way she could live with herself was to dull the pain, and that’s when the drugs took hold of her. She moved out of our grandparents’ house when she was sixteen but she came back every few days to see me. She always brought me something. Either a candy bar or a comic. She’d help me with my homework. She was always clean when she came visiting—or always looked clean—but sometimes she had the shakes, like she hadn’t had a fix in a few days. My grandparents were in the wrong generation to notice what was happening, and I was too young to know what caused it.
zh_text: 我沒有親人——母親死後，養大我跟貝琳達的祖父母也過世了；祖父死於心臟病，不久之後祖母因併發症和肺炎而去世，但最主要的原因則是寂寞。在所有人當中，我最希望貝琳達能來。小時候，父親還沒入獄前，貝琳達竭盡全力假裝我不存在，沒辦法假裝能讓我消失時，她會朝著我的方向丢來一句短短的話。發現父親的罪行後，她比較常跟我講話，但口氣更爲嚴厲。發現母親死在浴缸裡的時候，她握住我的手，輕撫我的頭髮，和我一起等警察來。那天她告訴我她很愛我，她會照顧我。當然，最後照顧我們的責任落到祖父母身上，但他們過得很辛苦。他們年紀大了，沒有錢讓我們過得很好，但他們也盡力了，免得我們被送去寄養家庭。貝琳達一向覺得我是她的責任。她比我大四歲，除了是姊姊，也要負起母親的責任，但到了晚上她不是姊姊也不是媽媽——她習慣在晚上溜出門，到街上賺錢，然後哭著回家，口袋裡裝滿骯髒的紙鈔，她會抱著我，告訴我一切都沒問題。最後還是出了問題，她痛恨自己的行爲，爲了活下去，只好讓自己麻木，這時她染上了毒癮。十六歲時她搬出祖父母家，不過每隔幾天就回來看我。她總會買東西給我，比方說糖果或漫畫。她會教我寫作業。來看我的時候她總是很正常，應該說看起來沒有毒癮，但有時候她的手會抖，似乎好幾天沒滿足毒癮。祖父母上了年紀，沒注意到她的情況，我太小了，不知道發生了什麼事。

en_text: Then one week she didn’t come to visit. Then another week went by. Eventually the cops came. It was like that Wednesday morning all over again. They pulled into the street and knocked on the door and my life changed the same way it had every other time I saw them.
zh_text: 然後，她一整個星期沒來，然後又過了一個星期。最後警察來了。就像父親被捕的那個星期三早晨重演了一次。警車停在路邊，警察過來敲門，每次看到他們，我的生命就改變了。

en_text: Sam is given a thousand hugs, almost all of them ending with the other person crying. Sam becomes numb to the tears. She’s adorable in her little black dress and makes me want to cry every time I see her. She knows what’s going on, but at the same time she doesn’t know. She’s been told Mummy has gone to Heaven, but a few times she’s asked if Mummy will be coming home over Christmas to visit. I wish I could cancel Christmas. I hate that the rest of the city gets something to enjoy.
zh_text: 大家都過來擁抱小珊，幾乎每個人都落淚了。小珊對眼淚已經很麻木。她一身黑色洋裝，非常可爱，每看她一眼，我就想要流淚。她知道我們在幹嘛，可是她不懂。我們告訴她媽媽去天上了，但她問了幾次媽媽會不會在耶誕節的時候回來看我們。我眞希望我能讓耶誕節消失。城裡其他人都在期待耶誕假期，令我滿心懫恨。

en_text: Jodie’s coffin is covered in flowers. Most of the church is. The accountant in me is wondering how much all of this is costing, and thinking how death must be the most profitable business in the world since we all get around to doing it sooner or later. The father inside of me holds Sam’s hand tightly the entire time, drawing strength from her. The man inside me hurts, he’s screaming inside, he’s dying inside, he’s confused, and he doesn’t know what his future holds. The service lasts an hour. People come out of it saying it was “nice,” but it’s not the word I’d use. I don’t know what it is. Certainly not nice. “Devastating,” might be better. “Confusing” would work too. “Nice” seems to trivialize it.
zh_text: 茱蒂的棺木蓋滿了鮮花，教堂裡放眼望去都是花。身爲會計師，我納悶這些花要多少錢，又忍不住想殯葬業一定是世界上最賺錢的行業，畢竟所有人早晚都要死。但我也沒忘了父親的身分，從頭到尾我都緊緊握住小珊的手，從她身上得到力量。而我也是茱蒂的丈夫，我覺得好痛，心中不斷呐喊，我快死了，我好困惑，我不知道未來會怎麼樣。儀式持續了一個小時。大家走出去的时候都說辦得很好，我絕對不會用好來形容。我不知道該怎麼說，但絕對不好。應該說造成了嚴重的破壞，或者令人混淆。光用一個好字，似乎太輕描淡寫了。

en_text: Six people carry Jodie’s coffin outside. Her dad, her two brothers, and three friends. Their faces are strained but I don’t think it’s from the coffin being heavy. Her brothers had to fly in from different parts of the country and tomorrow will fly back out. I keep a firm grip on Sam’s hand as we walk behind them. Sam keeps a tight grip on her teddy bear with the other hand. The coffin is shiny and new and sure won’t be that way in a few hours from now. I wonder how heavy it is, what kind of percentage of the weight is from my wife.
zh_text: 茱蒂由六個人抬到外面，她的父親丶兩名兄弟和三個朋友。他們的面孔繄繃，應該不是因為棺木很沉重。她的兄弟從紐西蘭其他城市搭飛機過來，明天又要搭飛機回去。跟著棺木前進時，我仍繄繄抓住小珊的手。小珊的另一隻手則繄繫抓住她的泰迪熊。全新的棺木閃閃發亮，過了幾個小時想必就會失去光澤。我不知道棺木有多重，有百分之多少的重量來自我的妻子。

en_text: We reach the hearse. It’s shiny and black, while death is dull and black. The rear door is open, waiting for her, waiting for the men to slide my wife inside as if they were furniture movers. The door closes, then we all seem to stand around for a minute or two, not really sure what to do next until we all kind of figure it out, and the hearse leaves and we follow it. We all drive in a row, our headlights on, Jodie leading the way. It’s about a kilometer of winding road between the church and Jodie’s new home so the drive is short and I’m not sure why no one walked. We find the missing occupants of the media vans about thirty meters from the grave, some with cameras set up on tripods, others on shoulder mounts. These people don’t have any respect for Jodie, or for Sam or for myself, and none at all for the situation. They don’t care about our loss, they care only about ratings, and the thing I know for certain in this world is that one day these people will become victims to their own stories. One day somebody, maybe some other son of a serial killer, will pick these vultures off one by one. But that day is in the future, and today Sam is the granddaughter of a serial killer, daughter of a murder victim, and the media are already speculating about her too. They call her cute and adorable, they call her loss a tragic one, and they wonder what kind of woman she will turn into—her life has this dark blemish now, and combined with her genes . . . they want to know what she will become. The same men who loaded Jodie in the hearse go about unloading her.
zh_text: 我們走到靈車旁，黑色的車身閃著光澤，對照的卻是黑暗陰沉的死亡。車尾打開了，等著茱蒂進去，等著那六個扮演搬家工人角色的男人把我妻子的棺木推進去。門關上了，衆人似乎呆站了一兩分鐘，不確定接下來要做什麼，最後大家都想到了，靈車開動，我們就跟在後面。大家的車排成一列，頭燈打開，茱蒂負責領隊。教堂和茱蒂的新家大約距離一公里，這條路彎彎曲曲，很快就到了，不知道爲什麼沒人用走的。新聞探訪車上的人原來都在這裡，距離墳墓大約三十公尺遠，有些人已經把攝影機和三腳架搭好了，有些人則扛在肩膀上。這些人不尊重茱蒂，也不尊重我跟小珊，更不尊重今天的場合。他們不在意我們失去了親人，他們只在乎收視率，我確信，總有一天他們也會變成受害者，要面對自己的人生故事。總有一天，會有一個人，或許也是連續殺人魔的孫女，謀殺案被害人的女兒，媒體已經開始推敲她的未來。他們說她很可愛，他們說她的遭遇很可憐，他們已經在懷疑她未來會變成什麼樣的人——她的生命現在有了這麼大的缺憾，再結合她的基因——媒體想知道她的未來。

en_text: My wife has become cargo, her final voyage about to begin. They carry her from the hearse to the grave, lowering her onto some weird scaffolding erected over the top of it. Father Jacob thinks of more he wants to add, then, at exactly 3:27 on a Monday afternoon, the scaffolding moves and my wife is lowered into the ground, the six men who carried her standing silent among the crowd, hurting, while the six men who did this to her spend their money in the streets of Christchurch, enjoying the beautiful summer’s day.
zh_text: 把茱蒂棺木放入靈車的人又把她搬下車。我的妻子變成了貨物，即將走上最終的旅程。他們把她從靈車搬到墳墓邊，放到墳墓上方搭起的怪異鐵架上。雅各神父想到一些他想補充的話，然後，就在星期一下午三點二十七分，鐵架移動了，我的妻子下降到墓穴裡，搬運她的六個男人靜靜站在群衆間，傷痛難當，而害死她的六個男人卻在基督城的街上花搶來的錢，享受這美好的夏日。

en_text: The bank manager is buried on the same day at a different cemetery. We don’t combine the events and hold one giant two-for-one funeral party to save money, or to make it easier on the media so they can save gas.
zh_text: 銀行經理同一天在另一座墓地下葬。我們不想爲了省錢合併辦理，然後舉辦大規模的雙人葬禮集會，更沒想到要幫媒體省油資。

en_text: We pick up handfuls of dirt and throw it onto the coffin. It’s a tradition I’ve never really understood. I’ve done it four times in the past: my mother, my sister, both my grandparents. Now my wife. I don’t ever want to have to do it again.
zh_text: 我們抓起一把土，撒在棺木上。我從不了解這項傳統有什麼意義。我撒過四次了：母親、姊、爺爺和奶奶。現在則是我的妻子。我再也不想撒土了。

en_text: The rest of the dirt is underneath a grass-colored piece of canvas, hidden away, and it’s another tradition I don’t understand. Are they worried the dirt will cement the reality that my blood-covered wife, funeral arrangements, and coffin could not? I don’t know. Maybe it’s the traditions that get people through the day.
zh_text: 其他的土則藏在草綠色的帆布下，這項傳統我也不懂。他們擔心那堆土就能證實我滿身是血的妻子已死，但葬禮的安排和棺木卻不代表什麼？我不懂。或許靠著傳統，才能讓我撐過這一天。

en_text: Sam picks up a small handful of dirt and sprinkles it onto the coffin. She doesn’t ask why. In fact she hasn’t asked anything at all today—she’s done what she’s been told, quietly following me since we woke up this morning.
zh_text: 小珊抓了一把土撒在棺木上。她沒有問爲什麼。事實上她今天什麼也沒問我們叫她做什麼她就照做，從一早起床就默默跟在我後面。

en_text: After the funeral we all drive to Jodie’s parents’ house. I look at the streets and the people and I want to leave this city and wish I’d done it years ago. The Christmas traffic slows us down—even at four o’clock on a Monday afternoon. Soccer mums are driving their kids around the city in SUVs and heading to the malls.
zh_text: 葬禮結束後，我們都把車子駛往茱蒂的父母家。看著街道，看著其他人，我很想離開這座城，希望我早在幾年前就離開了。耶誕節的車潮讓車速減慢即使現在是星期一下午四點鐘。全職媽媽開著休旅車把小孩送到城裡各處，然後前往購物中心。

en_text: There are about thirty cars parked in my in-laws’ street, and only two media vans. I have to park two blocks away. The distraction thing happens while I drive—I’ll see a car getting ready to run a red light and I’ll brake, I’ll avoid him, the moment passes, and then Jodie hits my thoughts with such brutality I almost burst into tears. My days are made up like that—the memory of her loss impacting on me over and over, trying to break me. Or maybe no longer trying—maybe succeeding.
zh_text: 岳父母住的那條街停了大概三十輛車，只有兩台新聞探訪車。我得停在兩個街口外的地方。開車的時候我會分心看到一台準備要闖紅燈的车子，我會踩下煞車避開他，那一刻過去了，對茱蒂的思念狠狠擊中我，眼淚幾乎奪眶而出。我的日子就這麼過失去她的記憶一再衝擊，想把我打垮。或者不用再試下去我已經垮了。

en_text: The weird food/funeral thing is taking place. It’s another of the traditions. It was the same when my mum and sister died, my grandparents cooking a thousand sausage rolls for the guests, cracking open bottles of lemonade and grape juice, swallowing down food and sorrow and sharing stories. The house is almost standing room only with the amount of people here, but they part for me and Sam, and I lead her through the living room and out onto the porch into the sun. I tell her to go and play in her playhouse but she doesn’t want to. She wants to keep holding my hand, and that’s okay with me. On and off during the afternoon she’ll smile at me like she’s in on some secret that I don’t know about. She thinks her mum is returning.
zh_text: 怪異的葬禮集會開始了，另一項傳統。我媽媽跟姊姊去世的時候也一樣，祖父母爲賓客準備了上千個熱狗捲，開了不知道多少瓶檸檬汁和葡萄汁，讓食物隨著悲傷嚥下，分享彼此的故事。來了這嬮多人，大家都只能站著，但看到我跟小珊，大家都讓路了，我牽著她穿過客廳，走到門廊上，浸潤在陽光裡。我叫她去遊戲屋裡玩，她不要。她要繼續牽著我的手，我當然不會拒絕。這天下午，她偶爾會對我微微一笑，彷彿她知道我不知情的小祕密。她覺得媽媽會回來。

en_text: “Mummy’s a ghost,” she said as Jodie hid under the sheets from her on the day she died.
zh_text: 「媽媽變成鬼了。」茱蒂用床單蓋住自己時小珊這麼說，就在那天茱蒂死了。

en_text: One by one the guests fade away. I’m given handshakes and hugs and words of condolence, and none of them help. I’d put any one of these people into the ground if it would bring Jodie back.
zh_text: 賓客一個一個離去。有人跟我握手，有人給我擁抱，有人向我說安慰的話，都沒有用。如果能用某人的命換回茱蒂，我願意把他埋到土裡。

en_text: In the end there’s only family—and none of it is mine, except my daughter. It’s Jodie’s family, and as much as I want to leave and never see them again, I can’t. None of this is their fault. None of it is my fault. I guess it’s just one of those things. That’s what murder is these days—just one of those things that happens, get used to it, deal with it, move on.
zh_text: 最後在場的只有親戚除了我女兒外，他們跟我都不是血親。他們是茱蒂的家人，我很想離開，不要再見到這些人，但我不能走。他們沒做錯事，我也沒做錯事。或许就是所謂的陰錯陽差。現在的謀殺有了新的形式有人被殺了，接納事實，處理問題，活下去。

en_text: Sam is finally out in the playhouse Nat built for her a couple of years ago. Nat spent twenty years as a builder and the last ten years running a hardware shop. I’m sitting out on the porch watching her when he comes out and hands me a beer. His suit jacket is gone, his sleeves are rolled up, and his tie is askew. He has big forearms with long white hairs, and big hands that he uses to pry the top off his beer. I suddenly realize for the first time that as hard as it is for me, it’s perhaps even harder for him.
zh_text: 小珊終於去遊戲屋玩了，兩年前納森幫她建了這座小房子。納森在營造業工作了二十年，過去十年則經營五金行。我坐在門廊上看小珊玩，他走出來，拿了一瓶啤酒給我。他脫掉了西裝外套，袖子捲得高高的，頜帶也歪了。他有粗壯的上臂，上面長滿長長的白毛，还有一雙大手，能輕鬆撬開啤酒瓶蓋。我突然發覺到，雖然我覺得很難受，或许對他來說更難受。

en_text: “Hell of a day,” he says, and he sits next to me at the outdoor table he built. “Yeah.”
zh_text: 「可怕的一天。」他坐到我旁邊，門廊上還有一張他做的戶外桌。「對。」

en_text: “Hell of a service. They did . . . a great job,” he says, maybe recognizing how hollow his words sound. “Notice how people came out of there saying the service was nice? I don’t know what the hell they mean by that,” he says. “I mean, I think I know what they mean, and I’ve probably said the same thing at other funerals. But the word doesn’t fit. Does that make sense?”
zh_text: 「可怕的葬禮。他們……還不錯，」他說，或許也發現了他的話有多空洞，「你發現了嗎？大家出來都說葬禮辦得不錯。我不知道他們是什麼狗屁意思。我的意思是，我知道他們是什麼意思，我去參加葬禮時可能也說過這種話。但很不恰當。你懂嗎？」

en_text: “Yeah.”

“I figure there’s no alternative, right? I mean, what the hell else are people going to come out saying? That it was a bloody awful service? That they had a bad time? That they had a great time? I guess it’s all you can say.”
zh_text: 「應該也沒什麼其他的好說了吧？我是說，不然大家參加完葬禮出來要說什麼？這場儀式糟透了？他們如坐針氈？他們覺得很好玩？我猜你也只能說不錯了。」

en_text: “I guess it is.”
zh_text: 「或许吧。」

en_text: He lifts the bottle up to his lips and takes a long swallow. “They’re going to catch those bastards,” he says. “I wish to hell they’d put me in a room with them one at a time. I wish . . . ah hell,” he says, and then, “I keep thinking I’m dreaming.”
zh_text: 他舉起瓶子喝了一大口。「警察會抓到那些王八蛋，」他說，「我眞希望他們讓我跟這些人一對一對幹。我眞希望……啊，他媽的。」他又接著說，「我一直覺得我在做夢。」

en_text: “I know.”
zh_text: 「我懂。」

en_text: Sam waves at us, then goes back to her world, talking to her teddy bears, maybe telling them about how nice the service was. Mummy’s a ghost. Yeah, maybe she’s talking to Jodie too.
zh_text: 小珊對我們揮揮手，然後回到她的世界裡，對著泰迪熊講話，或許要告訴它們葬禮辦得很好。媽媽變成鬼了。對，或许她也在跟茱蒂講話。

en_text: “You have to feel the same way, right? If you could get your hands on those people?”
zh_text: 「你也有同樣的感覺吧，對不對？如果你有機會對付那些王八蛋的話？」

en_text: I’d love it. The words don’t come out, thankfully, and they’re not even my words. I’m not sure whose they are. “I’d kill them,” I say, knowing that’s what he wants to hear, wondering if it’s actually something he thinks I’m capable of. Maybe he’s hoping I am.
zh_text: 我很想。還好這幾個字沒脫口而出，這也不是我想講的話。我不知道從何而來。「我要殺了他們。」我知道納森想聽這句話，不知道他是否眞以爲我能殺人。或许他希望我可以。

en_text: “It’s going to be hard, taking care of her yourself.” “I know.”
zh_text: 「不容易啊，你要自己照顧小珊。」「我知道。」

en_text: “But you’re a good kid,” he says. “You’ll do great. I know it. And, well, we’re always here for you.”
zh_text: 「但你是個好孩子，」他說，「你沒問題的，我知道，而且我們一定會幫忙。」

en_text: I open up my beer and take a long sip so I don’t have to speak.
zh_text: 我開了啤酒，喝了好一大口，避免回話。

en_text: “I know that you’ve always thought we didn’t think much of you. And I know why you think that. And I admit, in the beginning, it worried me when Jodie told us she was dating you and who your dad was. Shit, don’t think for a moment that we didn’t know it was unfair to think like that, I mean, we’re good people, we don’t have prejudices against anybody. Doesn’t matter who you are, you’re good to us, we like you. Could be anybody—hell, even gay people. But, well, you don’t imagine your daughter growing up and being with somebody whose father is a serial killer. And before you judge me on—”
zh_text: 「我知道，你一直以爲我們覺得你不怎麼樣。我也知道爲什麼。我承認，剛開始的時候，茱蒂告訴我們她在跟你交往，也說了你爸爸是誰，我眞的很擔心。媽的，别以爲我們不知道那樣很不應該，我是說，我們是好人，我們對別人沒有偏見。不論你是誰，我們都覺得你很好，我們很喜歡你。不然也有可能是別人嘍——說不定是同性戀，見鬼了。但是，你不會想到你女兒長大後居然跟連續殺人魔的兒子在一起。你先不要批評我……」

en_text: “I don’t judge you. I understand. I’ve lived with it my entire life.”
zh_text: 「我不會批評你。我懂，我這輩子就這麼過來的。」

en_text: “I know you have, son, and you don’t deserve it. But it is what it is, and you’ll go through it in ten years or more when Sam is old enough to date. Truth be told, I think we would have been fearful no matter who Jodie brought home. It took some getting used to, with your dad’s past and everything, but I want you to know how proud we are of you, and we love you and we know how happy you made Jodie, and we have a granddaughter who means the world to us. We wouldn’t have that precious little girl if you’d never met our Jodie.”
zh_text: 「孩子，我知道，你不需要受人歧视。但事實就是這樣，等過了十年吧，小珊到了可以約會的年紀，你也要經歷同樣的過程。說老實話，不管茱蒂跟誰約會，我們都會擔心。你爸爸那些事情要過了一段時間才會習慣，但我要你知道，我們非常以你爲傲，我們很爱你，我們也知道你讓茱蒂很幸福，我們也愛死了小珊。要是你沒碰到茱蒂，我們就沒有這麼可愛的外孫女了。」

en_text: I take another sip of beer, following his thought process, wondering if he chose those words specifically and hoping he didn’t. He’s saying they wouldn’t have Sam if it wasn’t for me. But he’s also saying they’d still have Jodie.
zh_text: 我啜了一口啤酒，遵循他的思路，不知道他是否刻意修飾過他的用詞，也希望他的話都發自内心。他說要是沒有我，就沒有小珊了。但他也說，要是沒有我，茱蒂就還在。

en_text: “I wanted to let you know how much we believe in you,” he says. “And that, well, we don’t blame you for what happened. We know how, how you called out, how you tried to stop them from shooting that woman.”
zh_text: 「我要告訴你，我們對你很有信心。」他說。「還有，我們一點也不怪你。我們聽說怎麼了，知道你喊出聲來，知道你想阻止搶匪射殺那個女人。」

en_text: “Jodie would still be alive if I hadn’t.”
zh_text: 「要是我沒開口，茱蒂就不會死了。」

en_text: He doesn’t answer for about twenty seconds. Just keeps working away at his beer. He wipes at his mouth and turns toward me. “I know,” he says. “Don’t think that I don’t know that. And part of me, part of me is angry at you for that. Part of me thinks if you’d kept your mouth shut, none of this would be happening.”
zh_text: 他沉默了二十秒，把啤酒倒入口中。他擦擦嘴巴，轉過身來看著我。「我知道，」他說，「不要以爲我不知道。我心裡——我心裡也有一點氣你。我心想，要是你乖乖閉嘴，就不會有這些事了。」

en_text: “Let me finish,” he says.
zh_text: 「先讓我說完。」他打斷我。

en_text: “But—”
